lessons.title: Ethereum is a world computer
lessons.content:
# Ethereum is a world computer

Bitcoin is a public notebook of who sent what. Ethereum is a public computer that also keeps a notebook. If you treat Ethereum as “Bitcoin with extra coins,” you will misread every contract, every token, and every failed transaction that still costs money.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say, in your own words, what **Ethereum** is for, why a computer is a better picture than a coin, and why Crystal Stones still lives on BNB Smart Chain even though the idea started here. This academy will not tell you to buy ETH, BNB, USDT, or Crystal Stones.

## A computer is not a coin

A **computer** is a machine that follows instructions and remembers results. Your phone is a computer. A bank’s ledger software is a computer. Ethereum is a computer that many independent machines run together, so the instructions and the memory are public.

**Ethereum** is a public network launched in 2015. Its bet was: let people publish small programs, called **smart contracts**, and let every machine on the network run the same program the same way. The notebook of transfers is still there. The new object is the program.

Bitcoin already had a limited script language. It was designed to move coins under simple rules, not to host shops, tokens, and games. Ethereum’s designers wanted a general machine. That is why people call it a **world computer**. The phrase is marketing-adjacent. The useful meaning is smaller: **one shared machine whose memory anyone can inspect, and whose programs anyone can call if they pay the fuel.**

A world computer is not a god. It does not know your name. It does not reverse a theft. It does not parent you. It runs the code that is already there.

## Programs sit on the same book as payments

In Basic you learned a **blockchain** is a public book of sealed pages. Ethereum still has blocks, hashes, and a writer rule. What changed is what a page can contain.

A Bitcoin-style page is mostly: “these coins moved from A to B.” An Ethereum-style page can also say: “call this program with these inputs, update its memory, maybe send some ETH, maybe emit a public receipt.” The page is still sealed. The computation is extra work the network agrees to do.

That is why Ethereum needs a **native coin** that is not just a souvenir. Computation costs machines time. The coin pays for that time. We will name that coin **ETH** in the next lesson. Hold the picture today: **payments and programs share one book.**

TABLE
Picture people sell | What the object actually is | What fails if you believe the slogan
Bitcoin 2 | A different public computer with its own book | You send value to the wrong chain because the address looks familiar
A faster bank | A public machine with no help desk | You expect a reversal that will not come
A company called Ethereum Inc | A protocol plus many apps on top | You trust a random website because it has a diamond logo
A token printer | A computer that can host many token programs | You assume every ticker on the screen is honest
ENDTABLE

## Shared memory is the new fact

When two bank apps disagree, you call support. When two Ethereum nodes disagree about what a program stored, the network’s rules pick one history. The **state** is the official memory: every account’s balance, every contract’s stored numbers, at this block.

**State** means: the current contents of the machine’s memory, agreed by the network. A transfer changes state. A successful contract call changes state. A failed call may change nothing in the program’s notebook and still burn the fuel you paid. Module 5 will unpack that failure. Today you only need: **the computer remembers.**

That memory is why a token can exist as a list inside a program. USDT on Ethereum is not a second chain. It is a program’s notebook of who is owed how many units. Crystal Stones on BNB Smart Chain is the same family of object, on a different computer that copied Ethereum’s design. This academy will not tell you to buy either one.

## What “world” does and does not mean

“World” does not mean every country recognised it as legal tender. It does not mean it is the only computer. It means the machine is public and global in the same way a public website is global: anyone with a connection can read it; anyone who can pay the fee can try to write.

There are other world computers now. **BNB Smart Chain (BSC)** is one of them. It copies Ethereum’s program format so the same style of contract can run, with BNB as fuel, on chain ID 56. Ethereum mainnet is chain ID 1. Same-looking addresses. Different books. Basic already trained that reflex. Intermediate will use it until it is boring.

**Worked scenario.** Ada the freelancer is paid in USDT. A client says “Ethereum is the real chain, send me your ETH address, I’ll send USDT.”

1. Ada does not hear “real” as a holiness ranking. She hears a **network name**.
2. She asks: which book — Ethereum mainnet, or BNB Smart Chain, or something else?
3. She checks which USDT she actually holds. Ticker letters are not a network.
4. She refuses to paste an address until the client names the chain and the token contract.
5. She remembers Crystal Stones’ published BEP-20 contract is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` — verify only, never a payment address, and not how this $10 Intermediate course is checked out. Checkout is USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.

DIAGRAM
                    PUBLIC COMPUTER (one book)
+------------------+     +------------------+     +------------------+
|  Ether transfers |     |  Smart contracts |     |  Token notebooks |
|  (native coin)   |     |  (programs)      |     |  (storage lists) |
+------------------+     +------------------+     +------------------+
         \                    |                    /
          \                   |                   /
           v                  v                  v
              sealed pages (blocks) everyone copies
              chain id 1 = Ethereum   chain id 56 = BSC
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this academy will not smuggle in

We will not rank Ethereum as morally better than Bitcoin. Bitcoin is a settlement notebook with a different job. We will not rank Ethereum as morally better than BSC. BSC is where this academy’s token lives, and where cheap practice transactions often happen.

We will not tell you Ethereum “replaced” banks. Adults still use banks. We will not tell you a smart contract is a legal contract. A **smart contract** is a program the network will run. A legal contract is a document courts understand. They can overlap. They are not the same object.

NOTE
Academy rule: “on Ethereum” is a location, not a blessing. A scam program can sit on a public computer just as calmly as a useful one. The chain will run both. Your job in Intermediate is to name the object — computer, account, program, token list — before anyone’s story.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are here so that Ethereum stops being a ticker and becomes a machine: public programs, shared memory, sealed pages. The next lesson names the fuel and the accounts. None of this is a shopping list.

## Say this out loud

- Ethereum is a public computer that also keeps a notebook, not “Bitcoin with extra coins.”
- A smart contract is a program the network will run, not a court document.
- State is the official memory of that computer at a given block.
- BNB Smart Chain copies this computer style on a different book (chain ID 56).
- Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 token on BSC to verify, not a payment address and not a buy order.

Next: accounts, state, and why ETH is the native coin of this machine.

lessons.title: Accounts, state, and why ETH is the native coin
lessons.content:
# Accounts, state, and why ETH is the native coin

A computer that cannot charge for work gets flooded with junk. Ethereum charges in **ETH**. ETH is not “the best coin.” It is the native fuel and the native balance of this particular machine.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate an **account** from a token row, say what **state** includes, and explain why a wallet can show USDT and still need ETH (or, on BSC, BNB) before anything moves.

## An account is a record the machine keeps

An **account** on Ethereum is an object the network tracks. It has an **address** — the 0x name — and a bundle of facts: how much ETH it holds, a **nonce** (how many transactions it has already sent), and, if it is a contract, the code and the stored data.

You already met addresses in Basic. They look the same family on Ethereum and on BNB Smart Chain: forty hex characters after 0x. Same shape. Different books. An account on chain ID 1 is not the account on chain ID 56, even if the letters match.

Two kinds of accounts exist. The next module is entirely about them. Today’s split is enough to use:

- **Externally owned account (EOA)** — controlled by a private key a human (or a company) holds. A wallet app such as Trust Wallet or MetaMask — examples of wallet apps, not endorsements — usually shows you this kind of account.
- **Contract account** — controlled by code. No seed phrase for the contract itself. People call it by sending it a transaction.

Both can hold ETH. Only the contract holds code. Token balances are usually not “the account is the token.” Token balances are numbers inside a token program’s notebook, labelled by your address.

## State is the whole memory, not your app screen

**World state** is the official snapshot: every account, every ETH balance, every contract’s storage, at a block. Your wallet is a view of a few rows. An explorer is a view of more rows. Neither is the whole machine.

When people say “the blockchain remembers,” they mean this state, updated page by page. A transfer of ETH changes two balances in state. A token transfer usually does **not** move ETH from sender to receiver as the payment. It asks the token program to rewrite two numbers in its storage. You still pay ETH (or BNB on BSC) as fuel to the network for the rewrite.

That is the Intermediate correction to a Basic shortcut. In Foundations, “sending a token” felt like sending a coin. Under the hood, you are paying the computer to edit a list.

TABLE
Object | Lives where | What your wallet shows | What you pay to change it
ETH (native coin) | The account’s own balance in state | “ETH” on Ethereum | ETH as value moved, plus ETH as gas
BNB (native coin on BSC) | The account’s own balance on chain 56 | “BNB” | BNB as value and as gas
USDT (token) | A number in the USDT contract’s storage, keyed by your address | “USDT” if the wallet knows that contract | Native coin for gas; the token program edits the list
Crystal Stones (BEP-20) | A number in its BSC contract storage | Only if you added the contract | BNB for gas. This academy will not tell you to buy it.
ENDTABLE

## Why a native coin must exist

If fuel were a token living inside a program, you would need that program to run in order to pay to run programs. That is a circle. Native coins sit **outside** token programs. The protocol itself knows the ETH balance of an account. It can subtract gas even if every token contract is broken.

**Gas** is the metering of computation. You will get a full lesson on it in Module 5. The Intermediate one-liner is: **every step the computer takes has a price in gas, and gas is paid in the native coin.**

This is why Ada can hold 500 USDT on Ethereum and still be stuck. If her ETH balance cannot cover gas, the token program will not be asked to move the 500. The same trap exists on BSC with BNB. People call it “I have money but I cannot send it.” They have a token row. They do not have fuel.

## ETH is not Crystal Stones, and Crystal Stones is not checkout

ETH is the native coin of Ethereum mainnet. Crystal Stones is a **BEP-20** token on BNB Smart Chain. Different computers. Different jobs. The published Crystal Stones contract — `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` — is a **verification string**. It is not a payment address. It is not how you pay for this course.

This Intermediate track is **$10 USDT on BEP-20 through academy checkout**. Not ETH. Not Crystal Stones token. Not a random 0x pasted in chat. Academy staff will never ask for a seed phrase or a private key to “activate” an account.

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper in a market group is told “pay the academy in Crystal Stones, here is the contract, send tokens there.”

1. He names the objects: Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 token to verify, not a checkout rail.
2. He names the real checkout: $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.
3. He does not send tokens to the contract address. Sending tokens to a contract that is not expecting them is how value sits in a notebook nobody has a withdraw button for.
4. He does not send ETH on Ethereum to “match” a BSC invoice.
5. He treats any chat that asks for a seed to “sync state” as theft.

DIAGRAM
STATE AT ONE BLOCK
+---------------------------+   +---------------------------+
| EOA 0xAda...              |   | Contract 0xUSDT...        |
| ETH balance: 0.04         |   | code: token program       |
| nonce: 12                 |   | storage:                  |
| code: (none)              |   |   0xAda -> 500 USDT       |
+---------------------------+   |   0xShop -> 20 USDT       |
                                +---------------------------+
Ada's wallet shows 500 USDT AND 0.04 ETH.
Without ETH, the 500 is a number she cannot rewrite.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Misconceptions that will cost you this week

- “My wallet has USDT, so I can pay any USDT invoice.” No. Name the chain.
- “ETH and BNB are the same because both pay gas.” They pay gas on **different** computers.
- “State is whatever Telegram says arrived.” State is what the explorer shows for that chain’s book.
- “A native coin is a token with a fancier logo.” Native coin is protocol-level. Token is a program’s list.

NOTE
Academy rule: never confuse a token row with fuel. If a screen shows a dollar-named token and a near-zero native balance, you are looking at a parked number, not a ready payment. Practice with tiny amounts. Prefer a test send. This classroom will not give price targets for ETH or anyone else.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are here so that “balance” splits into three ideas: native coin, token row, and the fuel needed to change either. Next we look inside the machine — the EVM as a stack, not a motivational flowchart.

## Say this out loud

- An account is a record the machine keeps: address, native balance, nonce, and maybe code.
- State is the official memory at a block, not a screenshot.
- ETH is Ethereum’s native coin and its gas money. BNB plays that role on BSC.
- A token balance is a number in a contract’s storage, keyed by your address.
- This course’s checkout is $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout, never the Crystal Stones contract.

Next: the EVM as a picture you can actually hold — a stack machine, not only a flowchart.

lessons.title: The EVM as a picture (stack, not only a flowchart)
lessons.content:
# The EVM as a picture (stack, not only a flowchart)

People draw Ethereum as a flowchart because flowcharts look like “steps.” The machine that actually runs a contract is closer to a **stack of plates** plus a notebook. If you only learn the flowchart, you will not understand gas, reverts, or why a “simple send” and a “contract call” are different jobs for the same computer.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to point at three boxes — stack, memory, storage — and say which one survives after the transaction ends.

## The EVM is the shared processor

The **Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)** is the rule-book for how every node runs contract code. **Virtual machine** means: a pretend processor defined in software, so many different physical computers can get the same answer.

BNB Smart Chain runs an EVM-compatible processor. That is why the same style of contract, the same 0x addresses, and the same wallet apps can talk to both chains. Compatible is not identical. Chain ID, native coin, validators, and the actual programs deployed are different. The processor family is the same.

You do not need to write bytecode. You need the picture of what the processor has on its desk while a call runs.

## Three places data can sit

While a contract runs, data lives in more than one drawer.

**Stack.** A last-in, first-out pile of small numbers the processor uses as scratch. Push a number on top, pop a number off the top. Most EVM operations eat values from the stack and push results back. This is why this lesson refuses a flowchart-only picture: the machine is stacking, not walking a poster.

**Memory.** A temporary workspace for the current call. It starts empty-ish, expands as the program writes into it, and **vanishes when the call ends**. Useful for building a string, copying calldata, preparing a return. Not the contract’s long-term notebook.

**Storage.** The contract’s durable notebook in world state. Writing storage is expensive in gas because every node must remember it forever (or until it is changed again). This is where token balances live. This is where an “owner” address is saved.

There is also **calldata**: the input bytes that arrived with the transaction, cheap to read, not a place the contract stores a diary.

TABLE
Place | Lives through the call | Lives after the block | Typical job
Stack | Yes, as plates on a pile | No | Arithmetic, jumping, feeding the next instruction
Memory | Yes, as a scratch pad | No | Temporary bytes for this call only
Storage | Yes | Yes — it is state | Balances, owners, allowances, config
Calldata | Yes, as the input | The tx is in history; the bytes are not “the contract’s diary” | Function name plus arguments
ENDTABLE

## A flowchart hides the cost

A flowchart says: “check balance, then subtract, then add.” The EVM says: load a storage slot onto the stack, compare, maybe **revert** (undo this call’s state changes, still charge gas for work already done), maybe write two storage slots, maybe append a log.

**Bytecode** is the compact instruction list the processor actually runs. Humans write **source** in a language such as Solidity. Compilers turn source into bytecode. Explorers may show source if someone uploaded it. The network does not run the comments. It runs bytecode.

When a wallet says “Contract Interaction,” it is telling you the EVM will execute bytecode, not merely move native coin. That is why the gas estimate is higher than a simple ETH send, and why a bug in the program can take your tokens without a second human in the room.

**Worked scenario.** A student wants to “just swap” inside a wallet app.

1. She sees a flowchart in a thread: connect, approve, swap, done.
2. She names the stack picture instead: the swap program will read storage, write storage, maybe call another program, and emit logs.
3. She checks she has native coin for the whole path, not only for the last box of the flowchart.
4. She remembers an **approve** is its own storage write — a permission in the token’s notebook — not a decoration.
5. She does a tiny test on the correct chain before any amount she would miss.

DIAGRAM
EVM DESK (one call)

  calldata (input bytes)
           |
           v
  +------------------+     +------------------+
  | STACK            |     | MEMORY           |
  |  [ top plate   ] |     |  scratch bytes   |
  |  [ next plate  ] |     |  die when call   |
  |  [ next plate  ] |     |  ends            |
  +------------------+     +------------------+
           |
           |  SLOAD / SSTORE (expensive)
           v
  +------------------+
  | STORAGE          |  <-- survives in world state
  |  slot 0: owner   |
  |  slot 1: supply  |
  |  map: addr->bal  |
  +------------------+
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why Intermediate learners need this picture

Without the stack picture, these sentences sound like superstition:

- “Failed but I paid gas.” Work happened. Revert undid storage writes. Fuel still burned.
- “Verified source.” Someone published text that matches bytecode. That is not an audit. Module 6.
- “The contract holds my USDT.” Your token row is in the token contract’s storage. A second contract may have **allowance** to rewrite that row.
- “BSC is Ethereum.” Same processor family. Different desk, different book, different native fuel.

NOTE
Academy rule: you will not be asked to write Solidity in this course. You will be asked to stop treating a contract call as a mysterious arrow. If you can point at stack, memory, and storage, you can later read an explorer without worshipping the green tick.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a desk picture of the EVM: a stack processor with temporary memory and durable storage. That picture will carry Module 3 (what a contract holds) and Module 5 (why gas numbers look the way they do).

## Say this out loud

- The EVM is a shared pretend processor. BSC is EVM-compatible, not the same chain.
- The stack is a pile of plates the processor uses while running.
- Memory dies at the end of the call. Storage is the notebook that remains.
- Token balances live in storage, which is why they survive and why they cost gas to change.
- A flowchart of “approve then swap” hides extra storage writes and extra ways to fail.

Next: Ethereum versus BNB Smart Chain, as geography, not as a fan war.

lessons.title: Ethereum vs BNB Smart Chain
lessons.content:
# Ethereum vs BNB Smart Chain

Same-looking addresses. Same-looking wallet screens. Two books. Intermediate starts failing the day you treat them as nicknames for one computer.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to compare Ethereum mainnet and BNB Smart Chain on the facts that actually bite: chain ID, native coin, explorer, gas habits, and where Crystal Stones lives. This academy will not tell you to buy ETH or BNB.

## Two computers, one family of tools

**Ethereum mainnet** is chain ID **1**. Native coin **ETH**. Public explorer **Etherscan**. Writer set: proof-of-stake validators on Ethereum’s rules.

**BNB Smart Chain** is chain ID **56**. Native coin **BNB**. Public explorer **BscScan**. Writer set: a more concentrated validator design you already met in the BSC beginner course.

Both run EVM-style programs. That is why MetaMask and Trust Wallet — examples of wallet apps, not endorsements — can add both networks. That is why a contract written for Ethereum can often be deployed on BSC. **Often** is not **already there**. A program exists only on the chain it was deployed to. Copying the idea is not copying the instance.

Crystal Stones is a **BEP-20** token on BSC. BEP-20 is BSC’s name for the ERC-20-style interface. The published contract to **verify**, never to pay, is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. If someone shows you a Crystal Stones contract on Ethereum, you are looking at a different object until proven otherwise.

## What is copied, and what is not

Copied: address shape, transaction shape, gas metering, ABI idea, token interface style, wallet UX.

Not copied: the state, the native coin, the explorer’s database, the validator set, the list of deployed contracts, the price of gas in local units, the social layer of “what people actually use this book for.”

A USDT you hold on Ethereum is a row in Ethereum’s USDT contract. A USDT you hold on BSC is a row in BSC’s USDT contract. Same nickname on the bottle. Different notebooks. Basic taught this. Intermediate repeats it because Intermediate is where people move $10 and $100 and then invent a story about “the chain ate it.”

TABLE
Fact | Ethereum mainnet | BNB Smart Chain
Chain ID | 1 | 56
Native fuel | ETH | BNB
Explorer | Etherscan (example of a public window) | BscScan (example of a public window)
Token style | ERC-20 and many others | BEP-20 (ERC-20-style) and many others
Where Crystal Stones is published | Not the home this academy verifies | BEP-20 contract on BSC, verify only
Typical beginner gas feeling | Often dearer | Often cheaper — still not free, still not a reason to skip checks
ENDTABLE

## Cheap gas is a feature and a lure

BSC’s cheaper gas is why this academy can ask you to practice with tiny amounts without turning every test into a painful fee. It is also why fake tokens, fake airdrops, and copycat contracts breed there. Attackers like cheap books too.

Ethereum’s dearer gas does not make a contract honest. A verified scam on Etherscan is still a scam. “I paid a lot in gas” is not an audit.

**Worked scenario.** An auntie is sending value to a niece at university.

1. The niece says “send USDT, here is my address” and pastes 0x…
2. The auntie asks which chain the niece’s wallet is actually watching.
3. They open the matching explorer — Etherscan for chain 1, BscScan for chain 56 — from a bookmark.
4. They send a tiny test on that one chain, wait for the explorer to show it, then send the rest.
5. They do not “try the other chain because the address looks the same.” Same letters, different book, missing funds.

DIAGRAM
WALLET SCREEN (looks identical)

[ Network: Ethereum  chain 1 ]     [ Network: BSC  chain 56 ]
[ Address: 0xAda...          ]     [ Address: 0xAda...          ]
[ Token list: local to this  ]     [ Token list: local to this  ]
[ Fuel needed: ETH           ]     [ Fuel needed: BNB           ]
              \                               /
               \                             /
                v                           v
         Etherscan history            BscScan history
         (not interchangeable)        (not interchangeable)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Binance is not BNB Smart Chain

**Binance** is an example of a centralised exchange. An exchange account is an IOU in a company ledger. BNB Smart Chain is a public book. BNB the coin is used as fuel on that book and also appears as an asset on the exchange. Three objects. Mixing them is how people withdraw to the wrong place and then argue with a help desk that cannot unwrite a public page.

If you buy USDT on an exchange and withdraw, you must pick the network the exchange offers that matches the book your wallet is on. “USDT” on the withdraw screen is a multiple-choice question, not a unique object.

NOTE
Academy rule: name four things before you send — asset, chain ID, explorer, fuel coin. If any of the four is guessed, stop. Crystal Stones’ contract is a verify-only string on BSC. Intermediate checkout is $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout, not a transfer to that contract.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are here to kill the last remaining “it’s all crypto” sentence. Ethereum and BSC are sibling computers. Siblings do not share a bank account. Next we draw the boundary of this course so you know what Intermediate will not pretend to teach.

## Say this out loud

- Ethereum is chain ID 1 with ETH as fuel. BSC is chain ID 56 with BNB as fuel.
- Same address letters do not move value across books.
- EVM-compatible means a similar processor, not a shared state.
- Crystal Stones is verified as a BEP-20 on BSC, not as a checkout address.
- Cheap gas on BSC is not a honesty stamp, and dear gas on Ethereum is not one either.

Next: what this course will teach, and the list of things it will refuse to pretend.

lessons.title: What this course will and will not teach
lessons.content:
# What this course will and will not teach

Intermediate is where academies get greedy. They start teaching you to “deploy” and “farm” and “get in early.” This course will not. It will teach you to see the objects well enough that a lie has fewer places to hide.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to tell a friend what six modules buy them, what they still will not be, and how this $10 track is actually paid for.

## What you should be able to do by the last quiz

After six modules you should be able to:

- Explain Ethereum as a public computer, not Bitcoin 2.
- Split **EOA** from **contract account** when an explorer shows the same 0x shape.
- Say what a contract stores — code, storage, maybe native coin — without calling it a vault of magic.
- Name ERC-20 and BEP-20 as interfaces, not as religions.
- Read gas, ABI, and explorer tabs well enough to catch a bad approval or a failed-but-paid transaction.
- List the common ways this design hurts people: unlimited approvals, fake tickers, “verified” as theatre, upgradeable proxies.

You should **not** expect to be a Solidity developer, an auditor, a trader, or a recovery agent.

## What this course refuses

We will not give buy or sell targets. We will not invent yield. We will not invent listing dates. We will not treat Crystal Stones’ mineral-vault story as proven because it is printed on a site. That story is **their claim to verify**.

We will not teach you to message a “recovery team.” Academy staff will never ask for a seed phrase, a private key, 2FA codes, or remote screen control. Anyone who does is not this academy.

We will not teach you that a smart contract is a substitute for a lawyer. We will not teach you that BscScan’s green tick is an audit. We will not teach you to pay this course in Crystal Stones token.

TABLE
You might want | This course gives | This course refuses
A job in Web3 | Vocabulary and failure cases | A placement, a salary, a “hiring partner”
A way to pay Intermediate | The fact: $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout | A Crystal Stones address, an ETH invoice, a chat-paste 0x
An audit of Crystal Stones | How to verify a contract address on BscScan | A certificate that minerals sit in a vault
Trading skill | Why tokens can be faked and drained | Entries, leverage, signals
Developer skill | What bytecode, ABI, and storage are | A Solidity bootcamp
ENDTABLE

## How the $10 actually works

This course is **paid Intermediate**. Price is **$10 USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)** through **the checkout processor**. That sentence is complete. It does not include ETH. It does not include the Crystal Stones token. It does not include a personal wallet an instructor pasted in WhatsApp.

The Crystal Stones contract `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` is listed in this academy so you can **verify** you are looking at the published BEP-20 asset. Verification is not payment. If a checkout page ever tells you to send Crystal Stones to that contract, the page is wrong or hostile.

Practice, when we ask for it, is tiny amounts you can lose, preferably on a **testnet** — a practice computer that looks like the real one and uses worthless play coins. Testnet is Module 6’s habit, not a playground for rent money.

**Worked scenario.** A student finished Basic and wants Intermediate.

1. She checks the course card: level intermediate, price $10, paid track.
2. She looks for the checkout processor USDT BEP-20, not a DM.
3. She ignores a Telegram admin who says “pay in CS token for a discount.”
4. She does not send USDT to the Crystal Stones contract “to whitelist.”
5. She starts Module 1 knowing this classroom is education, not a shop.

DIAGRAM
PAYING FOR THIS COURSE (the only picture)

[ Learner ] -- $10 USDT BEP-20 --> [ the checkout processor checkout ]
                                              |
                                              v
                                    access to Intermediate

NOT this:
[ Learner ] --> Crystal Stones token --> 0xe252... contract
[ Learner ] --> ETH on Ethereum     --> a chat address
[ Learner ] --> seed phrase         --> "support"
ENDDIAGRAM

## The voice you should expect

Adult. Direct. Short sentences, then one longer unpacking paragraph. Every heavy term defined the sentence after it appears. Ordinary people in the examples: Ada the freelancer, a shopkeeper, a student, an auntie sending naira. Not crypto-Twitter prophets.

When a token appears, this academy will not tell you to buy. When Trust Wallet or MetaMask appears, they are examples of wallet apps. When Binance appears, it is an example of a centralised exchange.

If a lesson feels like a glossary, it has failed. If a lesson feels like a rally, it has failed. Intermediate is a seeing course.

NOTE
Academy rule: you are not behind if you still have to look up chain ID 56. You are behind if you send value because a stranger was in a hurry. Use this course as a brake, not as a dare.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

This is the map and the ethics in one place, so later modules can go faster without smuggling a shop. Next module: the two kinds of accounts, which is the first place explorers quietly lie by looking identical.

## Say this out loud

- This course teaches Ethereum as a computer, accounts, contracts, tokens, gas, ABI, explorers, and common failures.
- It does not teach trading, Solidity-as-a-job, or recovery-agent magic.
- Checkout is $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.
- Crystal Stones’ contract is verify-only, never a payment address.
- Academy staff never ask for seed phrases, private keys, or remote control.

Next: two kinds of accounts — the key-holder and the program — and why they share an address shape.

modules.title: Two kinds of accounts
modules.description: The 0x string is a name, not a species. Externally owned accounts are key-holders. Contract accounts are programs. Gas is always paid by a signer. Explorers show both as addresses, which is why people send value into the wrong object.

lessons.title: Externally owned accounts
lessons.content:
# Externally owned accounts

If you can open a wallet app, type a password, and tap Send, you are looking at an **externally owned account**. The chain does not know your face. It knows a key.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what an EOA is, what it stores, what it cannot do by itself, and why academy staff will never ask for the secret that controls it.

## The object, without the app chrome

An **externally owned account (EOA)** is an account controlled by a **private key**. A private key is the secret that can create a digital signature. A **signature** is proof that the holder of that secret authorised a message, without putting the secret on the wire.

The public face of the EOA is the **address**. On Ethereum and on BNB Smart Chain the address is a 0x string derived from the public key. Your wallet app — Trust Wallet and MetaMask are examples of wallet apps, not endorsements — is a tool that holds the secret, shows a view of the book, and asks you to approve signatures.

The EOA itself, on the chain, is a small record: ETH (or BNB) balance, a **nonce**, and empty code. **Nonce** here means a counter of how many transactions this account has already sent. It stops a signed payment being replayed like a photocopied cheque.

An EOA does not contain your USDT. It does not contain Crystal Stones. Those are rows in token contracts. The EOA is the actor that can **ask** those contracts to rewrite their lists, if you sign.

## What only an EOA can do

On these EVM chains, a transaction that starts a change must be signed by an EOA (or by a specialised successor design; this course stays with the classic picture). A contract cannot wake up by itself and pay the grocer. Someone signs. Gas is paid by that signer.

That is why “the contract will automatically send me money every Friday” still needs a trigger: a person, a keeper bot, or another contract called by a person. There is no little employee living inside the program.

It is also why phishing works. If an attacker gets the private key or the **seed phrase** — the word list that reconstructs the key — they *are* the EOA. The chain will accept their signature as yours, because the chain never met you.

TABLE
EOA fact | What it means | Failure if you skip it
Controlled by a key | Whoever has the secret can sign | Sharing a seed is handing over the account
Has a nonce | Each send uses the next number | Copy-pasting an old signed tx can be replayed if nonce allows
Holds native coin | ETH on Ethereum, BNB on BSC | Token rows without fuel cannot move
Has no code | It cannot run a program of its own | You cannot “install protection” inside a normal EOA
Looks like 0x… | Same shape as a contract address | Sending to the wrong species of 0x
ENDTABLE

## Wallet apps are not the account

The account is on the book. The app is a lens and a signing room. If you import the same seed into a second app, you did not clone the coins. You made a second lens on the same EOA. If you install a fake app, you may be signing in a hostile room.

Binance, as an example of a centralised exchange, does not usually give you the EOA’s private key for the coins you “see” in the app. That balance is an IOU in their ledger until you withdraw to an address you control. Withdrawal is the moment you choose an EOA (or a contract) on a named chain.

**Worked scenario.** Ada the freelancer is paid to an EOA she controls.

1. She writes down that the object is an EOA on a named chain, not “Ada’s Binance.”
2. She funds a little native coin for gas before she needs to move a token.
3. She sends a tiny test to a shopkeeper who already received a test from her last month.
4. She never photographs the seed “just to be safe in chat.”
5. She treats any email from “MetaMask support” asking to confirm the seed as theft. Real wallet makers, and this academy, do not need those words.

DIAGRAM
WHO CONTROLS WHAT

[ Ada's brain ]     [ Wallet app (example only) ]     [ EOA on the book ]
  remembers            holds key encrypted               address 0xAda
  seed offline         asks Ada to tap Sign              ETH/BNB balance
       |                       |                         nonce
       |                       |                         code: none
       +---- must stay --------+---- signatures -------->+
            with Ada                go to the network
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this object is not good at

An EOA cannot enforce a company policy by itself. It cannot do “two directors must sign” unless you move to a contract (a multisig). It cannot freeze itself after a theft. It cannot call customer care.

That limitation is the point of self-custody and also the job. Basic already said you are the security team. Intermediate names the team’s badge: **holder of the EOA key**.

Crystal Stones’ contract is not an EOA. It is a program. Do not send tuition there. Tuition is $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout. This academy will not tell you to buy ETH, BNB, or Crystal Stones to “activate” an EOA.

NOTE
Academy rule: staff will never ask for a seed phrase, private key, or screenshot of a recovery screen. If a lesson asks you to practice, it asks you to sign a tiny transaction you initiated, on a chain you named, to an address you checked twice.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now point at an EOA as a key-controlled actor with a nonce and a native balance. Next: the other species — contract accounts — which share the 0x costume and none of the key story.

## Say this out loud

- An EOA is an account controlled by a private key, not by Solidity.
- The wallet app is a signing room. The account lives on the book.
- Nonce counts sent transactions so signed messages are not photocopies.
- Token balances are not stored inside the EOA; the EOA asks token contracts to edit lists.
- Anyone with the seed is the account. Academy staff will not ask for it.

Next: contract accounts — programs that can hold value and run code when someone knocks.

lessons.title: Contract accounts
lessons.content:
# Contract accounts

A **contract account** is an account whose “will” is bytecode. Nobody types a password for the contract itself. People and other contracts **call** it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a contract account contains, how it gets created, and why “the contract stole from me” is sometimes accurate and sometimes a mislabel for “I signed a call.”

## Born from a deployment, not from a seed

You create an EOA by holding a key. You create a contract by sending a special transaction that includes **init code**. The network runs that code once. The result is a new account with a new address, stored **bytecode**, and initial **storage**. That birth transaction is a **deployment**.

The address is still a 0x string. It is computed from the deployer’s address and nonce (or from other recipe rules for newer create operations). You cannot look at the letters and see “this one is a program.” You look at the explorer’s “Contract” tab, or at the code field in state.

Once born, the contract sits there. It does not browse the web. It does not wake at 9am. It waits. When an EOA (directly, or through another contract) sends it a call, the EVM runs its bytecode.

## What the contract account actually holds

Three families of thing:

- **Code** — the program. Empty on an EOA. Present on a contract.
- **Storage** — the durable notebook. Owner, total supply, mapping of balances, pause flags.
- **Native coin balance** — ETH on Ethereum, BNB on BSC. A contract can hold fuel-money. Holding it does not mean the contract knows a kind way to give it back. Withdrawal is a function someone must have written.

Token inventory is usually not “the contract is USDT.” For a token contract, the inventory of users is *inside* its storage. For a shop contract, it may also have been given allowance to move users’ tokens, or it may hold tokens in its own address’s row in the token contract. Those are different pictures. Module 3 and 4 separate them.

TABLE
Contract holds | Everyday translation | How people misread it
Bytecode | The rules that will run | “I read the website, so I read the rules”
Storage | The current notebook | “The tweet is the current notebook”
ETH / BNB | Native coins at the contract address | “It is a bank; I can demand a refund”
A row in another token | Tokens credited to the contract’s address | “Those tokens are safe because they are in a contract”
ENDTABLE

## Contracts do what they were written to do, including harm

A **smart contract** is a program the network will run. It is not automatically smart. It is not automatically a legal contract. If the program says “when Ada calls transfer, move her row to the shop,” it will do that when Ada signs. If the program says “when anyone calls drain, send everything to owner,” it will do that too.

Some contracts are **proxies**: a thin program that delegates to another program, so the team can later point at new logic. That is an upgrade path. It can be honest engineering. It is also how “immutable” becomes a slogan. Module 6 treats proxies as a way people get hurt.

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper is asked to “deposit into the staking contract.”

1. He opens BscScan or Etherscan for the correct chain and pastes the address.
2. He checks whether the explorer shows Contract, code, and a balance of native coin.
3. He looks for functions whose names sound like withdraw, not only deposit.
4. He refuses to sign if the only story is a screenshot of APY. This academy will not invent yield.
5. He practices, if at all, with an amount that can vanish without taking school fees.

DIAGRAM
CONTRACT ACCOUNT (cutaway)

+----------------------------------------------+
| Address: 0xShop...                           |
| Native balance: 0.8 BNB                      |
|                                              |
|  CODE (bytecode)     STORAGE (notebook)      |
|  +--------------+    +-------------------+   |
|  | how to call  |    | owner: 0xAdmin    |   |
|  | how to pay   |    | deposits[Ada]=50  |   |
|  | how to stop  |    | paused: false     |   |
|  +--------------+    +-------------------+   |
|                                              |
|  No seed phrase. Waits for a signed call.    |
+----------------------------------------------+
ENDDIAGRAM

## Who is “the contract” in a crime story

When funds leave, the explorer shows a from and a to. If your EOA signed `approve` and later a hostile contract pulled tokens, the token contract’s storage changed because **you previously authorised it**. If you sent native coin to a contract with no withdraw function, the coin is at that address and may sit there. If a proxy was upgraded, the new code may not be the code you read last month.

None of these require a seed theft. That is why Intermediate exists on top of the safety course. Basic taught “do not share the words.” Intermediate teaches “do not sign every knock.”

Crystal Stones is a contract on BSC. Verify `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. Do not treat it as a cashier. Do not treat a copycat contract with the same name as the project.

NOTE
Academy rule: a contract account is not a person you can persuade. You cannot email it. You cannot shout. You can only call the functions that exist — and on some contracts, only if you are already on a privileged list. Read before you send. Tiny amounts. Named chain.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now describe a contract account as code plus storage plus maybe native coin, born by deployment, awake only when called. Next: why explorers still print the same 0x costume for both species, and how to tell them apart in thirty seconds.

## Say this out loud

- A contract account is controlled by bytecode, not by a seed phrase.
- Deployment is the birth transaction that stores the program.
- Contracts can hold ETH or BNB and still have no honest way to give it back.
- “The contract stole from me” sometimes means “I signed a call the code allowed.”
- Verify Crystal Stones on BSC; never pay tuition to that contract.

Next: addresses look the same, the objects do not — a comparison you will reuse on every explorer tab.

lessons.title: Addresses look the same, the objects do not
lessons.content:
# Addresses look the same, the objects do not

Ethereum did not pick a different spelling for programs. That is a design choice and a trap. The 0x string is a **name**. The object behind the name is either a key-holder or a program.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to tell the two apart on Etherscan or BscScan, and you should refuse the sentence “I sent it to the address, so it arrived” until you name the species.

## The costume is forty hex characters

Both EOAs and contracts use the same address format on EVM chains. Copy-paste does not warn you. Chat apps do not warn you. A QR code does not warn you. The explorer does, if you look.

On Etherscan or BscScan, an EOA page typically shows a balance, a transaction list, and **no Contract tab with bytecode**. A contract page shows a Contract tab, often a token profile if it is a token, sometimes a warning banner, sometimes “Proxy.” Learn those tabs. Do not learn the logo in the chat header.

A second costume problem: the same 0x letters can be typed on Ethereum and on BSC. That is two names on two books, not one object with a dual citizenship. Lesson 4 in Module 1 already compared the chains. This lesson adds species on top of geography.

TABLE
What you see | EOA | Contract
Address shape | 0x plus 40 hex | 0x plus 40 hex
Code on the explorer | None | Bytecode, maybe verified source
How value gets in | Someone sends, or an exchange withdraws | Someone sends, or a function mints/credits
How value gets out | Owner signs a send | A function must exist and succeed
Who you “talk” to | A person or company with a key | A program, plus whoever holds admin keys
ENDTABLE

## Sending to the wrong species

Three common mismatches:

1. **You meant a person, you used a token contract.** Sending USDT to the USDT contract address is not “topping up USDT.” It is giving tokens to the program’s own row. Many token contracts cannot retrieve that. The units can sit there.
2. **You meant a checkout, you used a verify-only contract.** Crystal Stones’ published address is for verification. Sending CS tokens or USDT there as “academy fees” is the wrong object. Fees are $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.
3. **You meant Ethereum, you used BSC (or the reverse).** Same letters. Wrong book. The destination species might even differ: a contract on one chain can be unused space on the other.

**Worked scenario.** A student copies “the USDT address” from a blog.

1. She notices the blog did not say chain ID.
2. She pastes the 0x into BscScan and into Etherscan, separately.
3. On one explorer it is a token contract with millions of holders. On the other it may be empty, or a different thing, or nothing useful.
4. She does not send “to see what happens.”
5. She asks the payee for a screenshot of their **EOA** receiving page on the explorer, plus chain name, plus a tiny test.

DIAGRAM
SAME SPELLING, TWO SPECIES

0xA11CE...                         0xC0DE...
+------------------+               +------------------+
| EOA              |               | CONTRACT         |
| key somewhere    |               | bytecode         |
| nonce, fuel      |               | storage notebook |
| code: (empty)    |               | maybe admin key  |
+------------------+               +------------------+
        ^                                  ^
        |                                  |
   "send me your address"          "the official contract"
   might mean this                 might mean this

If you mix the arrows, the book still settles.
ENDDIAGRAM

## The explorer’s thirty-second check

Open the real explorer from a bookmark.

- Does it say **Address** only, or **Contract**?
- Is there a **Token** tracker? Then it is probably a token program, not your cousin.
- Is there a **Creator** and a creation transaction? Contracts have a birth tx. EOAs do not have a “deployment.”
- Is **Read/Write Contract** present? That is a program interface, not a person.
- Does the URL still say etherscan.io or bscscan.com, not a lookalike?

If a stranger refuses to let you do this check, they are asking you to skip the only cheap verification you have.

## Name tags are social, not cryptographic

Explorers let people attach **name tags** — “Tether: USDT Stablecoin,” “Binance 14,” “Crystal Stones.” A tag is a label an indexer or a community member published. It is not a signature from the contract. Scammers buy lookalike tags on fake windows. Even on a real explorer, a tag can be wrong, late, or copied onto a clone.

Treat a tag as a hint to go read the Contract tab and the creation transaction. Do not treat it as a passport. The academy’s Crystal Stones string is still the hex, not the words “Crystal Stones” in a header.

## First-seen is not a birthday for EOAs

Contracts have a creation transaction. EOAs often “first appear” when they receive value or send their first tx. That first-seen date is not a KYC file. A brand-new EOA can be honest. A three-year-old EOA can be a thief’s. Age is not character. Species plus the job you are doing is the check.

NOTE
Academy rule: an address is not an instruction. The instruction is: asset, chain, species (EOA or contract), function if it is a contract, amount you can lose. Missing any one of those, you do not send.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You will stop treating 0x as a personality. Next: who pays gas when the program runs, because the signer and the contract are easy to mix once the call starts hopping.

## Say this out loud

- Address format is a costume. Species is EOA or contract.
- The explorer’s Contract tab is the tell, not the letters.
- Sending tokens to a token contract is often a well.
- Same 0x on chain 1 and chain 56 are not one object.
- Crystal Stones’ 0xe252… is a contract to verify, not a person to pay.

Next: who pays gas when a contract runs — spoiler: the signer, not “the blockchain for free.”

lessons.title: Who pays gas when a contract runs
lessons.content:
# Who pays gas when a contract runs

A contract has no salary. When its code runs, **someone’s EOA pays gas**. If you cannot see who is paying, you do not understand the call.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to trace a simple call and a nested call, name the **msg.sender** idea in beginner language, and explain why a failed swap still took BNB or ETH.

## The signer starts the meter

A transaction has a **from**: the EOA that signed. That account pays the gas in native coin. The **to** may be another EOA (simple send) or a contract (a call). If it is a call, the EVM starts running bytecode. Every instruction eats **gas**. Unused gas can return. Used gas is gone, even if the program **reverts**.

**Revert** means: undo this call’s state changes, return an error, still charge for the work done. Beginners hear “failed” as “free.” The book is more precise: **failed to change the notebook, succeeded at billing the meter.**

On Ethereum the meter is paid in ETH. On BSC it is paid in BNB. Token rows do not pay the meter. That is why a wallet full of USDT and empty of BNB is parked.

## Nested calls still have one payer at the edge

Contracts can call contracts. A router calls a pair. A pair calls a token. From inside, each hop has a **sender**. The original human-visible payer is still the EOA that signed the first transaction. That EOA’s native balance is what the protocol subtracts for gas.

Beginner language for two jargon words you will see on explorers and in ABI tabs:

- **msg.sender** — the account that directly called this program this hop. Could be your EOA, or another contract.
- **tx.origin** — the EOA that signed the whole transaction. Intermediate learners should treat it as a warning label, not a tool to build with. Some hostile contracts trick old programs that trusted tx.origin.

You do not need to write those words in code. You need to know why a token transfer in the log might show the router as the sender, while your EOA paid the BNB.

TABLE
Question | Accurate answer | Popular wrong answer
Who pays gas? | The signing EOA, in native coin | “The contract pays; it has money”
Who can start a call? | An EOA signature (directly or via a wallet) | “The contract wakes up on a schedule by magic”
If the call reverts, is gas zero? | No. Work already done is billed | “Failed means refund”
If a router calls a token, who is msg.sender inside the token? | The router contract | “Always the human”
If Ada’s USDT moves, did she pay USDT for gas? | No. She paid BNB or ETH for gas | “USDT is dollars so it pays fees”
ENDTABLE

## Contracts can be funded and still not pay your gas

People see a contract holding 40 BNB and think “it will cover me.” Unless the code is written to refund gas (rare in the way beginners hope) or to pull tokens without your signature (dangerous, usually via allowance), that 40 BNB is the contract’s native balance, not your petrol station.

A **relayer** or **meta-transaction** service can pay gas on your behalf in some products. That is a company or a contract wrapping your intent. It is not the default. This course will not tell you to hunt “gasless” ads. Many are phishing.

**Worked scenario.** Ada tries a token swap on BSC.

1. The wallet estimates gas in BNB. She has USDT, almost no BNB. The tx cannot be sent.
2. She obtains a tiny amount of BNB as fuel — this academy still will not tell her to buy as an investment.
3. She tries again. The swap program reverts because of slippage. The explorer shows **Fail**. BNB decreased.
4. She does not open a support chat that asks for her seed to “refund gas.”
5. She reads the revert, lowers the ambition of the trade or walks away. She never pays Crystal Stones token as a “priority gas.”

DIAGRAM
ONE SIGNED TX, TWO HOPS

Ada's EOA  --pays BNB gas-->  Router contract
   (from)                         |
                                  | calls
                                  v
                             Token contract
                             (msg.sender = Router)
                             storage: Ada's USDT row changes

Ada's BNB: down (gas)
Ada's USDT: maybe down (if not reverted)
Router's "kindness": not paying her gas
ENDDIAGRAM

## Academy payment is not a contract call you invent

Paying $10 for Intermediate is a USDT BEP-20 transfer through academy checkout, not a custom contract you must “interact” with because a stranger said so. You should still keep BNB in the paying EOA for that USDT transfer’s gas. You should not send the $10 to Crystal Stones’ contract.

NOTE
Academy rule: if a helper offers to “cover your gas” in exchange for a seed, a remote-control app, or a prepayment to a random 0x, they are not a helper. Gas is cheap relative to a drained wallet. Pay your own tiny fuel.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now attach a human-visible payer to every contract animation. Next: reading an account on an explorer until the tabs are ordinary — EOA versus contract, native versus token, success versus fail.

## Say this out loud

- The signing EOA pays gas in the native coin, always, on a normal transaction.
- Nested calls do not move the gas bill onto the inner contract.
- A revert undoes notebook edits and still bills work done.
- USDT does not pay BSC gas. BNB does. ETH pays Ethereum gas.
- Nobody needs your seed to refund a failed swap.

Next: reading an account on an explorer — the practical exam for this whole module.

lessons.title: Reading an account on an explorer
lessons.content:
# Reading an account on an explorer

An explorer is a search engine for a public book. It is not a bank statement with a complaints department. If you learn five tabs, Module 2 is done.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to open Etherscan or BscScan from a bookmark, paste an address, and say whether you are looking at an EOA or a contract, what native coin it holds, which tokens the indexer noticed, and whether a recent transaction failed.

## Bookmark the real window

**Etherscan** is a widely used window onto Ethereum mainnet. **BscScan** is a widely used window onto BNB Smart Chain. They are examples of explorers, not sacred objects. Fake explorers exist. They will show green ticks for transfers that never happened.

Type the URL yourself. Do not click the first Google ad. Do not use the link in a giveaway tweet. Look at the certificate. Look at the chain ID hints. Then paste.

What you paste matters. An address, a transaction hash, a token name. Token name is the worst search. Names collide. Addresses collide much less if you copied the whole string. Crystal Stones you verify as `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BscScan, not as the first ticker result.

## The account header, slowly

At the top you will see the 0x, sometimes a name tag, a native balance, and a fiat estimate. Ignore the fiat estimate for decisions. It is a price feed, not a promise. This academy will not tell you to buy because a header is green.

Find:

- **Balance** — native coin. ETH or BNB depending on the explorer.
- **Tokens** — an indexer’s list of ERC-20 / BEP-20 rows. Indexers can be late. A missing token in this list is not always a missing token on chain.
- **Transactions** — calls this account sent or received.
- **Internal txs** — native coin moving because a contract’s code sent it, not because the human typed a simple transfer.
- **Token transfers** — the list edits inside token contracts.

If the page has **Contract**, you are in a program. If it offers **Read Contract / Write Contract**, that is ABI territory (Module 5). If it says **Proxy**, Module 6 applies before you deposit anything you care about.

## Token trackers are indexers, not the book

The Holders and Transfers tables on a token page are built by an **indexer** — software that watches logs and storage and paints a spreadsheet. Indexers can lag. They can miss a weird token that does not emit standard Transfer events. They can also paint a fake token beautifully.

When a shopkeeper wants to know if he was paid, the transaction hash on the real explorer is stronger than the token tracker’s top-of-page marketing. The tracker is a map. The hash is a specific event.

TABLE
Tab | What it is good for | What it is bad for
Overview | Species, native balance, first glance | Proving a token is a wise purchase
Transactions | Did this account sign or get called | Seeing token rows (use Token transfers)
Internal txs | Native coin moved by code | Understanding a token swap by itself
Token transfers | ERC-20 / BEP-20 list edits | Native coin sends
Contract | Bytecode, verified source, ABI | An audit, a legal opinion, a yield guarantee
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper thinks a customer paid 50 USDT.

1. He does not accept a screenshot. He asks for a transaction hash.
2. He opens BscScan from a bookmark (they agreed on BEP-20).
3. He pastes the hash. He checks Status = Success, To = his EOA or the correct payment contract, Token = the USDT contract he already verified, Amount = 50.
4. If Status is Fail, he has not been paid, even if the sender “spent gas.”
5. If the token name says USDT but the contract is unknown, he has been offered a fake. He does not ship goods.

DIAGRAM
EXPLORER PAGE AS A GRID (not a flowchart)

+------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
| HEADER           | NATIVE BALANCE    | TOKEN INDEX       |
| address, tags    | ETH or BNB        | many tickers      |
| EOA or Contract  | not your tokens   | not a blessing    |
+------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
| TX LIST          | TOKEN TRANSFERS   | INTERNAL TXS      |
| signed calls     | list edits        | code sending coin |
| success / fail   | which contract    | easy to miss      |
+------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
| CONTRACT TAB     | READ / WRITE      | LOGS              |
| code or empty    | ABI menu          | public receipts   |
+------------------+-------------------+-------------------+
ENDDIAGRAM

## What the explorer will not do for you

It will not reverse a send. It will not tell you if Crystal Stones’ RWA story is true. It will not tell you if an “owner” key is in honest hands. It will not replace the checkout processor. It will not warn you in a human voice when you are on chain 1 looking at an address that was quoted for chain 56.

It will, calmly, show that a contract is a contract. That is enough to prevent a surprising number of Intermediate-sized mistakes.

NOTE
Academy rule: practice reading explorers with tiny amounts and with addresses you already trust. Do not paste your seed into any explorer “decoder.” Explorers do not need it. Anyone who says they do is not an explorer.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 2’s skill is species recognition plus a gas payer plus a public window. Module 3 goes inside the contract: bytecode, source, ABI, storage, and native coin sitting in a program.

## Say this out loud

- Bookmark Etherscan for chain 1 and BscScan for chain 56. Do not trust random windows.
- Contract tab present means a program. Absent usually means an EOA.
- Token transfers are list edits. Native balance is a different object.
- A failed transaction can still cost gas and still not pay a shopkeeper.
- Verify Crystal Stones by contract on BscScan; pay this course in USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.

Next: a contract holds code AND value — three objects people mash into one word.
