lessons.title: Bytecode, source, and ABI are three objects
lessons.content:
# Bytecode, source, and ABI are three objects

People say “I read the contract” the way they say “I read the news.” They usually mean they read a website. The chain did not run the website. The chain ran **bytecode**.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate bytecode, source, and ABI, and you should know what “verified” on an explorer actually claims.

## Bytecode is what the EVM runs

**Bytecode** is the compact instruction list stored on the contract account. It is ugly on purpose. It is for the processor. When you “interact,” you are feeding this list.

If bytecode is empty, you are not looking at a contract. If bytecode is present, a program will run when called. You do not need to decode it by hand. You need to respect it as the only rules the network is committed to.

Teams can publish nicer text. The network does not require them to. Unverified contracts still run. Verified contracts still can harm you.

## Source is a human story that may match

**Source code** is the human-written program, often in Solidity. A compiler turns source into bytecode. **Verified source** on Etherscan or BscScan means: someone uploaded source, the explorer compiled it, and the result matched the bytecode on chain.

That match is useful. It lets you read function names instead of raw bytes. It is not an audit. An **audit** is a review by humans who look for bugs and still miss some. Verification is a compiler check. Module 6 will repeat this until it is a reflex.

Source can be flattened, minimised, or written in a style meant to look friendly. Comments are not executed. A comment that says “safe” does not constrain the bytecode.

TABLE
Object | Who it is for | What a match proves | What it does not prove
Bytecode | The EVM | This is the rule the nodes run | That the rule is kind
Source | Humans | If verified, this text compiled to that bytecode | That experts reviewed it, or that admin keys are honest
ABI | Wallets and explorers | How to encode function names and types | That you should click Write
Website | Marketing | Nothing about the chain by itself | Anything
ENDTABLE

## ABI is the menu, not the kitchen

**ABI** means **Application Binary Interface**. In beginner language: the menu of functions and argument types a wallet uses to cook calldata. “transfer(address,uint256)” is a menu line. The kitchen is bytecode.

If the ABI and the bytecode disagree, the wallet can show a friendly button that does something unfriendly. Verified explorers derive ABI from the source they matched. Unverified contracts can have an ABI pasted by anyone in your wallet. Pasting a hostile ABI is a known trick.

**Worked scenario.** A student wants to “read the Crystal Stones contract.”

1. She does not start at a Telegram PDF. She opens BscScan from a bookmark.
2. She pastes `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`.
3. She looks for bytecode (contract exists), then for a verified source match, then for the ABI-powered Read tab.
4. She treats that as geography and interface, not as a buy order. This academy will not tell her to buy.
5. She does not send USDT or CS tokens to that address as tuition. Tuition is the checkout processor, $10 USDT BEP-20.

DIAGRAM
THREE OBJECTS (side by side)

[ SOURCE TEXT ] --compiler--> [ BYTECODE ON CHAIN ]
   Solidity, comments            the only rules nodes run
   may be verified                  |
                                    v
                            [ ABI MENU ]
                            function names + types
                            wallets encode calldata

Website PDF ----x---- (no arrow to bytecode)
ENDDIAGRAM

## What to do when source is missing

Missing source is a fog, not a dare. You can still see native balance, token transfers, and the creation transaction. You cannot honestly say you read the rules. For Intermediate practice, skip unverified programs that ask for deposits. For Crystal Stones verification, you use the published address and whatever BscScan actually shows — you do not invent a friendlier PDF and call it source.

Some teams verify late. Some never verify. Some verify an old implementation while a proxy points elsewhere. Always look at the address you were given, not the address you wish they had given.

NOTE
Academy rule: “I read the contract” must mean “I opened the explorer, I saw bytecode, and if source was verified I read the functions that matter.” It must not mean “I liked the logo.” This classroom will not pretend those are the same sentence.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have three labels that Intermediate learners must keep un-mashed. Next: storage — the notebook that actually holds balances, owners, and the numbers a call will change.

## Say this out loud

- Bytecode is what the EVM runs. Comments are not bytecode.
- Verified source means a compiler match, not an audit.
- ABI is the menu wallets use to encode calls.
- A website is not one of the three objects.
- Crystal Stones is verified by address on BscScan, never paid as tuition.

Next: storage is the contract’s notebook — slots, mappings, and why writes cost.

lessons.title: Storage is the contract's notebook
lessons.content:
# Storage is the contract's notebook

If bytecode is the rules, **storage** is the current pencil marks. Token balances live here. So do owner addresses, pause flags, and allowances. When a transaction “does something,” it is usually rewriting this notebook.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what storage is, why it is expensive to change, and why a wallet screen is a translated view of a few slots.

## Durable, public, metered

**Storage** is the contract’s long-term data in world state. It survives after the call. Every full node must remember it. That is why a storage write costs more gas than adding two numbers on the stack.

The EVM does not store “Ada: 50 USDT” as a cute label. It stores **slots** — 32-byte buckets — and uses recipes (hashes of keys) for maps such as balances[address]. You do not need the hashing recipe. You need: **there is a bucket; a function knows how to read and write it; you probably cannot see the bucket without a tool.**

Explorers sometimes show decoded storage if source is verified. Sometimes they show raw slots. Wallets show a prettier translation: “50 USDT.” The translation can be wrong if the wallet is pointed at the wrong contract. The slot on the named chain is the object.

TABLE
Notebook item | Typical storage meaning | How a wallet translates it
balances[Ada] | How many token units Ada is credited | “50 USDT” or “50 CS”
allowance[Ada][Router] | How many units Ada allowed Router to move | Hidden until you inspect approvals
owner | Address allowed to call admin functions | Usually not shown on the home screen
paused | A boolean that may block transfers | You discover it when a send reverts
totalSupply | Units that exist according to this program | “Circulating” on a website, which may be poetry
ENDTABLE

## Reading is cheap; writing is the decision

**Read** calls (eth_call / “Read Contract”) ask a node to run a view function and return a number. They do not cost you gas if you are only asking. They also do not change the notebook.

**Write** calls are transactions. They cost gas. They can change storage. They can fail. They can also change storage in a way you did not intend if you signed a function you did not understand.

This is why “I was only connecting my wallet” is sometimes a lie the interface told you. Connect can be a signature of login. Approve is a write. Swap is a write. Each write should be named.

## Empty slots are still slots

If a mapping has no entry for Ada, the EVM treats the read as zero. That is why a brand-new address “has 0 USDT” on a token contract without ever having met it. Zero is the default, not a special freeze. A later transfer into that key creates a non-zero slot. A later transfer out can return it to zero. Zero is not “deleted from the internet.” The program can still write that key again.

This is also why airdrops work: the token program writes a new key in its map. Your EOA did not opt in. Your storage in *that* contract changed. Your ETH/BNB drawer did not.

**Worked scenario.** An auntie is shown a dApp that “only needs a connection.”

1. She treats Connect as identity theatre, not as a bank login that moves funds by itself — but she still uses a small practice wallet.
2. The next popup says Approve. She names it: a storage write in the token contract’s allowance map.
3. She checks the explorer’s Write preview or the wallet’s raw permission: spender and amount.
4. She refuses unlimited amounts for a first meeting with a site.
5. She does not approve Crystal Stones token as a way to pay academy tuition.

DIAGRAM
NOTEBOOK (storage) versus SCRATCH (memory)

BEFORE CALL                         AFTER SUCCESSFUL WRITE
+----------------------+            +----------------------+
| slot owner: 0xAdmin  |            | slot owner: 0xAdmin  |
| map Ada -> 100       |            | map Ada -> 80        |
| map Shop -> 0        |            | map Shop -> 20       |
| allowance Ada,X = 0  |            | allowance Ada,X = 0  |
+----------------------+            +----------------------+
memory: empty at start              memory: discarded
stack: plates during run            stack: discarded
ENDDIAGRAM

## The notebook can be rewritten by admin functions

If storage includes owner, the owner can often set new fees, pause, mint, or point a proxy at new bytecode. Then the rules you “read” last month are not the rules the processor will run. That is not always evil. It is a power map. Ask who holds the owner key. If the answer is “the community” and three wallets hold everything, you have your answer.

Crystal Stones’ RWA story, if you meet it, is a claim about the world. Storage cannot prove a mineral vault. Storage can prove how the token program credits rows. Keep those proofs separate. This academy will not tell you to buy.

NOTE
Academy rule: if you cannot name which storage map a button will change — balance, allowance, owner — you are not ready to tap Write. Read is free. Write is a decision. Practice on tiny amounts.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now treat storage as the place of record inside a contract. Next: a full before/after of a call, so “state change” is a picture, not a vibe.

## Say this out loud

- Storage is the contract’s durable notebook in world state.
- Token balances and allowances are storage maps, not decorations in a wallet.
- Reads do not change the notebook. Writes do, and they cost gas.
- Admin keys can rewrite storage recipes you thought were fixed.
- A website’s circulating-supply graphic is not a storage slot.

Next: a call changes state — before and after, on one page.

lessons.title: A call changes state (before/after diagram)
lessons.content:
# A call changes state (before/after diagram)

A **call** is a request to run a contract’s function with some inputs. If it succeeds, storage and maybe native balances look different. If it reverts, the notebook should look like before, and the fuel still went.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to draw a before/after for a token transfer and for a failed call, and you should stop using the word “sent” for both.

## Success is a new snapshot

World state at block N is a snapshot. A successful transaction in block N+1 produces a new snapshot. Explorers show you the later snapshot plus a trace of what happened.

For a simple ERC-20 / BEP-20 transfer, the before/after that matters is two numbers in the token contract’s storage, plus Ada’s nonce, plus Ada’s native coin (gas). Ada’s EOA does not store the token. The token program stores Ada.

For a native ETH send, the before/after is two ETH balances and a nonce. No token program. Different object. Mixing these two pictures is how people think a token send “should have moved ETH.”

TABLE
Call type | Before | After success | After revert
ETH send | Ada ETH 0.10, Shop ETH 0.01 | Ada 0.09 minus dust gas, Shop 0.02 | Notebook restored; gas gone
Token transfer | Token map Ada 100, Shop 0 | Ada 80, Shop 20; Ada’s BNB down a little | Maps still 100 and 0; BNB down a little
Approve | allowance Ada,Router 0 | allowance = some number | allowance still 0; gas gone
Hostile drain after approve | Ada 80, allowance max | Ada 0, attacker 80 | If it did not revert, there is no after-magic
ENDTABLE

## Failure is not a time machine for gas

When bytecode hits a require that fails, the EVM **reverts** that call’s state changes. Native coin used as **value** in the call returns. Native coin used as **gas** for work does not return in full. The nonce of the signer still advances, because a transaction was included.

That is why Ada can see Fail, a lower BNB, an increased nonce, and unchanged USDT. All three facts can be true together. The explorer is not glitching. She paid to learn the program said no.

**Worked scenario.** A student tries to transfer 25 USDT BEP-20 to a shopkeeper.

1. Before: she notes BNB, USDT row, nonce, on BscScan.
2. She signs. The wallet warns about gas. She accepts a tiny test first — 1 USDT, not 25.
3. After success: token transfer tab shows 1 USDT to the shopkeeper’s EOA; her nonce +1; BNB slightly down.
4. She then sends the rest. She does not switch to Ethereum mid-way “because the address is the same.”
5. If a later send fails, she compares before/after instead of DMing a recovery account.

DIAGRAM
BEFORE                               AFTER SUCCESS
Ada EOA                              Ada EOA
  BNB 0.05                             BNB 0.049 (gas)
  nonce 7                              nonce 8
  code none                            code none

USDT contract storage                USDT contract storage
  Ada  25.00                           Ada  0.00
  Shop  3.00                           Shop 28.00

AFTER REVERT (alternate ending)
Ada EOA: BNB 0.049, nonce 8
USDT storage: Ada 25, Shop 3   <-- notebook unchanged
ENDDIAGRAM

## Internal calls make after harder to see

A swap is several afters in one transaction: allowances, two token maps, maybe a native transfer, logs. The explorer’s Token transfers tab lists the list-edits. Internal txs list native hops. Logs are the receipts (Module 5).

If you only look at the overview, you will miss a hop. Intermediate habit: open the hash, not only the address.

## Value field versus token field

On the explorer, **Value** usually means native coin attached to the transaction. A USDT transfer can show Value = 0 and still move 50 USDT in logs. Beginners read Value = 0 as “nothing happened.” They then argue with a shopkeeper who was, or was not, paid in a token.

Read both columns. Native value is one drawer. Token transfers are another. Internal txs are native hops caused by code. After a swap, all three can be busy. After a simple token transfer, Value is often zero and Token transfers is the whole story.

Crystal Stones transfers, if you ever inspect one for verification practice, are list-edits in that BEP-20 contract. They are not academy checkout. Checkout remains $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout. This academy will not tell you to buy CS because a before/after looks busy.

NOTE
Academy rule: write the before numbers down — even on paper — for the first dozen calls you make. Memory is a bad explorer. A two-line before/after will catch more thefts than a motivational video.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

State change is now a picture with two columns. Next: native coin sitting inside a contract, which is a third column people forget until they need a withdraw function that does not exist.

## Say this out loud

- A successful call produces a new snapshot of storage and balances.
- A token transfer’s before/after is in the token contract’s map, not inside the EOA.
- A revert restores the notebook and still spends gas; nonce still moves.
- Swap afters are multiple maps; read the hash, not only the address.
- “Sent” is a lazy word. Say what changed.

Next: ETH sitting inside a contract — value trapped, value intended, and how to tell.

lessons.title: ETH sitting inside a contract
lessons.content:
# ETH sitting inside a contract

A contract address can hold native coin the way an EOA can. On Ethereum that coin is ETH. On BSC it is BNB. Holding is not the same as being a bank.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain how native coin gets into a program, how it gets out, and why “I sent it to the contract so the team can refund me” is often a eulogy.

## In is easy; out is a function

Anyone can send ETH to most contracts. Some contracts have a receive or fallback function that accepts it. Some do not, and a direct send reverts. Some accept tokens but not ETH. The explorer’s native balance is the residue of whatever the code allowed in, minus what it allowed out.

**Out** requires bytecode that can transfer native coin to an address, and a caller allowed to trigger it. If that function is missing, the ETH is **stuck**. Stuck is a real Intermediate word. It does not mean “the team is processing it.” It means there is no instruction the EVM can run to move it.

This is why you do not send native coin to a token contract “to add liquidity” unless you are using the actual function a protocol provided, on the correct chain, with amounts you can lose. Random 0x + ETH is not liquidity. It is a donation to the void.

TABLE
Situation | Native coin at contract | Can a user get it back?
A well-written payable shop with withdraw | Yes, some | If you call the right function and are allowed
A token contract you used as a cashier | Often accidental | Often no
A proxy that was upgraded | Maybe | Maybe not under the new code
A honeypot that accepts deposits | Yes, growing | No, by design
Your EOA | Yes | Yes — you sign a send
ENDTABLE

## Tokens sitting at a contract are a different drawer

If a contract’s address is credited inside a USDT program, that is a token row, not ETH. A contract can be rich in USDT and poor in ETH. It may be able to move the USDT if it has code to call transfer, and unable to move ETH if nobody wrote withdraw.

People mash these drawers together because wallets show both on one screen. Keep them split: native drawer, token drawer, storage drawer.

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper is told “send BNB to the Crystal Stones contract to whitelist Intermediate.”

1. He names the contract: `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`, verify only.
2. He names the actual checkout: $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.
3. He does not send BNB there. He does not send CS token there. He does not send USDT there.
4. He understands any BNB that arrived in a program with no withdraw for him is not a “pending whitelist.”
5. He reports the chat as hostile, not as a payment delay.

DIAGRAM
TWO DRAWERS AT THE SAME 0x

Contract 0xC0DE...
+-----------------------------+
| NATIVE DRAWER               |   ETH or BNB at this address
|  12.4                       |   leaves only if bytecode sends it
+-----------------------------+
| TOKEN DRAWER (in USDT map)  |   USDT credited to 0xC0DE
|  800 USDT                   |   leaves only if bytecode calls USDT
+-----------------------------+
| STORAGE DRAWER              |   owner, flags, user records
+-----------------------------+

Ada sending "to the contract" must name which drawer she is filling.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Payable, receive, fallback — only as warning labels

You may see those words on verified source. **Payable** marks a function that may accept native coin. **Receive** is the function for a plain send. **Fallback** is the “if nothing else matched” function. You do not need to write them. You need to treat unknown payable doors as extra ways to throw value into a program.

On BSC, replace ETH with BNB in every sentence of this lesson. The trap is identical. The fuel coin is different. The explorer is BscScan.

## Self-destruct and other vanishing tricks

Some old patterns let a contract send its remaining native coin to a target and remove its code. You do not need the opcode name as a hobby. You need the Intermediate warning: **a contract that held ETH last month may be empty and even sourceless today.** Do not send “because the screenshot from March showed a balance.” Read the header today.

Upgradeable proxies complicate this further: the door address remains, the kitchen changes, the native drawer may still be at the door. Module 6. Today: look at the live native balance, look for a withdraw function, do not donate.

NOTE
Academy rule: never send native coin or tokens to a contract unless you can name the function that is supposed to handle it and the function that would let you exit. If you cannot name both, you are donating. Donations are allowed. Accidental donations should not be how you pay $10 tuition.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now see value-at-a-contract as a drawer problem, not as a customer-care problem. Next: who set the drawers up — constructor, owner, admin keys.

## Say this out loud

- Contracts can hold ETH or BNB. Holding is not a refund policy.
- Value leaves a contract only if bytecode can send it and someone is allowed to trigger it.
- Token rows at a contract are a different drawer from native coin.
- Do not send funds to Crystal Stones’ contract as checkout or whitelist.
- Stuck is a technical word. It is not “pending.”

Next: constructor, owner, admin keys — the humans behind the program.

lessons.title: Constructor, owner, admin keys
lessons.content:
# Constructor, owner, admin keys

A program has a birth and, often, a boss. Intermediate learners who skip the boss will memorise bytecode that can be steered.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a constructor did once, what an owner can still do, and why “decentralised” on a banner does not erase an admin key.

## Constructor runs once, at birth

The **constructor** is code that runs at deployment, then disappears from the live runtime in the usual Solidity picture. It sets the first storage: owner, token name, initial supply, a treasury address.

If the constructor set owner to the deployer’s EOA, that EOA is the boss until a transfer of ownership happens. If it set owner to a **multisig** — a contract that requires several signatures — that is a different boss, often healthier, still a boss.

You can find the birth on the explorer as the **contract creation** transaction. The “From” is the deployer. The deployer is not always the current owner. Owners can change if the code allows.

## Owner is a storage slot with extra rights

**Owner** usually means an address allowed to call restricted functions: mint, pause, set fees, upgrade a proxy, withdraw native coin, blacklist. There is no law that the word must mean that. You read the functions. But as a working default, owner is power.

**Admin keys** is the broader phrase: any privileged secret or address — owner, minter, pauser, proxy-admin, “operator.” A project can have many. A project can hide them behind names like “governance.” Governance with three wallets is a group chat.

TABLE
Power | Honest use | Hostile or sloppy use
Mint | Issue units under a published policy | Print until early holders can exit
Pause | Stop a bug while patching | Trap users in a notebook
Set fee | A shop’s commission | A surprise tax on sells
Upgrade | Fix a bug | Swap in a drain
Withdraw | Retrieve operating funds | Empty user deposits
ENDTABLE

## How to look without becoming a detective-cosplay

On a verified contract, open Read: owner(), admin(), hasRole if it uses roles. Open Write and see which functions are restricted — you will not call them. Check whether ownership can be **renounced** (set to a dead address). Renounce is a claim you can verify later; it is not holiness. A team can still hold other keys.

For Crystal Stones, treat any owner or admin you find as part of **verification**, not as a reason to buy or a reason to send tuition. This academy will not tell you to buy. The RWA story remains their claim. Admin keys cannot prove a vault. They can prove who may change the token program.

**Worked scenario.** Ada is shown a “community token, no owner.”

1. She opens the explorer, Contract, Read.
2. She finds owner() returning a non-zero address. The banner was false.
3. She finds pause() and mint() in the ABI.
4. She does not deposit. She does not argue on Twitter. She leaves.
5. She still would not have paid Intermediate in that token. She uses the checkout processor USDT BEP-20.

DIAGRAM
BIRTH AND BOSS (layers)

Layer 4  Website: "community run"
Layer 3  ABI: mint, pause, upgrade   <-- extra rights
Layer 2  Storage: owner = 0xAdmin
Layer 1  Bytecode deployed at birth
Layer 0  Constructor ran once, set layer 2

If layer 4 disagrees with layer 2, layer 2 wins.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What a boss cannot do

An owner cannot reverse a token you already sent to a thief’s EOA, unless the token program has a freeze/clawback and they choose to use it. Some regulated token contracts can freeze. Many cannot. Do not assume a parent.

An owner cannot recover Ada’s seed. An owner cannot make BscScan lie to the whole network (they can name-tag, which is social). An owner cannot turn Crystal Stones into the the checkout processor cashier.

NOTE
Academy rule: always ask “who can still change this?” If the answer is a key, you are using a product with a company-shaped risk, even if the chain is public. That can be acceptable. Calling it unstoppable is not acceptable.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is complete when you can name code, notebook, native drawer, and boss. Module 4 puts tokens on that stage as ERC-20 and BEP-20 interfaces — including USDT and Crystal Stones as objects to distinguish, not as shopping.

## Say this out loud

- The constructor runs at deployment and sets the first notebook.
- Owner and other admin keys are extra rights in storage.
- Banner words lose to Read functions on the explorer.
- Mint, pause, upgrade, withdraw are power — honest or hostile depending on who holds them.
- Verify Crystal Stones; do not pay it. Checkout is USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.

Next: tokens — ERC-20 and BEP-20 — a token is not a coin.

modules.title: Tokens: ERC-20 and BEP-20
modules.description: A token is a program’s list, not a native coin. ERC-20 and BEP-20 name the same style of interface. Decimals, supply, and allowances are how that list is kept. USDT, Crystal Stones, and ETH are three different objects. Tickers are not identity.

lessons.title: A token is not a coin
lessons.content:
# A token is not a coin

**ETH** is a coin of the Ethereum computer. **BNB** is a coin of BNB Smart Chain. A **token** is a row in a program’s notebook. If you use one word for both, you will pay gas with the wrong object and verify the wrong 0x.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say that sentence without a slide deck, and you should refuse ticker-only talk.

## Native coin is protocol-level

The protocol knows how much ETH an account holds. No token contract needs to run for that number to exist. Gas is subtracted from it. A simple send moves it. That is a **native coin** (sometimes called the native currency of the chain).

A **token** needs a contract. The contract’s storage map says how many units each address is credited. Moving a token is calling that program. If the program is paused, the token does not move even if you have fuel. If the program is a fake, the ticker still says USDT.

This academy already used USDT as a BEP-20 token in Basic. Intermediate adds the mechanical reason: **you were always editing a list.**

TABLE
Object | Kind | Fuel to move it | Identity
ETH | Native coin on Ethereum | ETH (value + gas) | The protocol’s ETH
BNB | Native coin on BSC | BNB | The protocol’s BNB
USDT on BSC | BEP-20 token | BNB for gas | A specific contract on chain 56
USDT on Ethereum | ERC-20 token | ETH for gas | A specific contract on chain 1
Crystal Stones | BEP-20 token | BNB for gas | 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 to verify, not to buy
ENDTABLE

## Why wallets make this harder

Wallet home screens put native coin and tokens in one list with logos. Logos are not identity. Anyone can deploy a token named ETH, USDT, or Crystal Stones. The wallet may even pick a logo from a public list if the name matches. That is a courtesy. It is not a notary.

Adding a token by contract address is the adult move you learned on BSC. It is the same move on Ethereum. You are telling the lens which notebook to read. You are not summoning coins from the void.

## Wrapped coins are still tokens

You will meet **WETH** and **WBNB**. **Wrapped** means: a token program that credits you a row when you lock native coin in it, and burns the row when you unwrap. It is a token, not the native coin. It can pay in places that only speak ERC-20 / BEP-20. It cannot pay gas. Sending WBNB to someone who asked for BNB is the coin/token mix-up wearing a synonym.

This academy will not tell you to wrap, unwrap, or farm anything. The only reason the word appears is so you do not treat “ETH” in a token list on BSC as Ethereum’s native coin, and so you do not treat WBNB as fuel.

**Worked scenario.** An auntie sees “500 USDT” in two wallets.

1. Wallet A is watching Ethereum. Wallet B is watching BSC.
2. She names two notebooks. She does not add the numbers together.
3. She checks each contract on the matching explorer.
4. She will pay a shop on BSC from the BSC row, with BNB as gas.
5. She will not tap a random “ETH” token on BSC and treat it as native ETH.

DIAGRAM
COIN versus TOKEN

NATIVE COIN                         TOKEN
+------------------+                +------------------+
| Protocol balance |                | Contract storage |
| in the account   |                | map[address]     |
| pays gas         |                | cannot pay gas   |
| simple send      |                | must call program|
+------------------+                +------------------+
        ^                                   ^
        |                                   |
   ETH on chain 1                      USDT / CS rows
   BNB on chain 56                     only on the chain
                                       that contract lives
ENDDIAGRAM

## This academy will not tell you to buy

Not ETH. Not BNB. Not USDT as an investment pitch. Not Crystal Stones. USDT appears here because it is how many invoices, including this $10 Intermediate checkout through academy checkout, are denominated on BEP-20. That is a payment fact, not a yield story.

Crystal Stones remains a BEP-20 asset with a published contract to verify. The mineral-vault story is their claim. A token is still not a coin even if the story is about rocks.

NOTE
Academy rule: say the full object every time — “USDT BEP-20 on BSC,” “ETH native on Ethereum,” “Crystal Stones BEP-20, verify-only contract.” If a sentence uses only a ticker, rewrite it before you send.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The coin/token split is the floor of Module 4. Next: the actual interface — the small list of functions that make something ERC-20 or BEP-20 shaped.

## Say this out loud

- A native coin is protocol-level and pays gas. A token is a program’s list.
- Tickers and logos are not identity. Contracts and chain IDs are.
- USDT on Ethereum and USDT on BSC are two notebooks.
- Crystal Stones is a token, not a coin, and not checkout.
- Wallets list both kinds on one screen. You must still split them.

Next: the ERC-20 / BEP-20 interface — the menu that almost every token you meet is claiming to follow.

lessons.title: The ERC-20 / BEP-20 interface
lessons.content:
# The ERC-20 / BEP-20 interface

**ERC-20** is a style of menu for tokens on Ethereum. **BEP-20** is BSC’s name for the same style of menu. An **interface** here means: a published list of functions and events wallets expect. It is not a government licence.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name the core functions, say what “compatible” means, and know that a menu can be implemented in a hostile kitchen.

## The menu people actually mean

The core ERC-20 / BEP-20 functions you will see on Read/Write tabs:

- **totalSupply** — how many units the program says exist.
- **balanceOf(address)** — that address’s row.
- **transfer(to, amount)** — rewrite two rows, if the sender has enough.
- **approve(spender, amount)** — set an **allowance**.
- **allowance(owner, spender)** — read that permission.
- **transferFrom(from, to, amount)** — a spender moves someone else’s row, up to the allowance.

Plus names people treat as metadata: **name**, **symbol**, **decimals**. Metadata is how wallets print “USDT” and “18.” Metadata can be copied by a fake.

**BEP-20** adds some BSC-flavoured optional pieces in the original spec talk, but in practice you will treat BEP-20 tokens as ERC-20-style lists on chain 56. Crystal Stones is in that family. This academy will not tell you to buy it.

TABLE
Function | Who usually calls it | What storage it touches | Beginner danger
transfer | You, from your EOA | Two balance rows | Wrong to-address, wrong token contract
approve | You | Allowance map | Unlimited spender rights
transferFrom | A router or shop | Balances plus allowance | You already signed the permission
balanceOf | Anyone (read) | None (read) | Reading the wrong contract
name / symbol | Anyone (read) | None (read) | Fakes copy these first
ENDTABLE

## Compatible is not honest

A program can implement the menu and still:

- take a fee on transfer (“tax token”)
- block some addresses from selling
- let the owner mint
- pause
- lie in name() while being a different object

Wallets will still show a ticker. DEXs may still list a pair. The interface is a plug shape. It is not a character reference.

**Worked scenario.** A student is asked to “just approve USDT.”

1. She opens the token contract on BscScan — the USDT she actually holds, not a lookalike.
2. She sees approve and transferFrom on the ABI. She names the pair: approve writes permission; transferFrom spends it.
3. She checks the spender address is the shop or router she intended, on chain 56.
4. She sets a tight amount, not unlimited, for a first interaction.
5. She does not approve the Crystal Stones contract as a substitute cashier for Intermediate.

DIAGRAM
INTERFACE (menu) versus IMPLEMENTATION (kitchen)

Menu (ERC-20 / BEP-20)
  balanceOf | transfer | approve | transferFrom
                    |
                    v
Kitchen (bytecode) can be:
  [ honest list ]   [ tax + pause ]   [ honeypot ]
                    |
                    v
Wallet still prints the same ticker if name() matches
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why this interface took over

Because wallets can build one Send screen. Because shops can take many tokens with one integration style. Because BSC could copy Ethereum’s homework and get MetaMask-shaped tools on day one.

The cost of that success is ticker collision. Everyone implements name() as “USDT” or “Crystal Stones.” Your defence is the contract address plus the chain, not the menu heading.

## transfer versus transferFrom is a job question

If you are paying a person’s EOA, **transfer** is the honest path: you push tokens. If a shop’s website must pull, it will ask **approve** so it can **transferFrom**. Pull is not automatically theft. Unlimited pull is a standing debit. Intermediate habit: ask whether this job needs a pull at all.

Custodial apps and some invoices use pull so they can charge an exact amount after a quote. the checkout processor for this course is still “send USDT BEP-20,” not “approve the Crystal Stones contract.” If a page asks you to approve CS token to unlock Intermediate, the page is wrong.

NOTE
Academy rule: when a site says “ERC-20 payment,” you still ask which chain. Ethereum ERC-20 USDT is not BEP-20 USDT. the checkout processor for this course wants USDT BEP-20. The interface name is not the destination.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now treat ERC-20 / BEP-20 as a plug, not as a halo. Next: decimals, supply, allowances — the three numbers people misread on every token page.

## Say this out loud

- ERC-20 is an Ethereum token menu. BEP-20 is the BSC-flavoured twin.
- transfer moves your row. approve writes a permission. transferFrom spends that permission.
- Implementing the menu does not make a token honest.
- name() and symbol() are copyable labels.
- Crystal Stones is BEP-20 on BSC to verify, not a buy and not tuition.

Next: decimals, supply, and allowances — the arithmetic that makes screens lie.

lessons.title: Decimals, supply, allowances
lessons.content:
# Decimals, supply, allowances

Token screens are translations. The chain stores integers. Wallets insert a decimal point. Approvals store a permission integer that can be larger than your balance, larger than the supply, larger than sense.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to decode those three numbers and catch two lies: “I approved 0 so I am safe” when a leftover allowance exists, and “total supply is market cap.”

## Decimals are a display choice stored as a number

**Decimals** is usually an 18, a 6, or sometimes something weirder. It means: take the integer in storage and shift the point that many places for humans.

USDT on many EVM deployments uses 6 decimals. So 1,000,000 in storage displays as 1.00 USDT. A token with 18 decimals stores 1 followed by 18 zeros for one displayed unit. If you copy the raw integer into a send box that expects display units, you may send everything.

Wallets usually hide this. Explorers sometimes show raw. Read functions show raw integers. Intermediate learners look twice when a number looks like a phone number.

## Supply is what the program says exists

**totalSupply** is a storage value the program reports. It is not automatically locked. If mint exists, supply can rise. If burn exists, it can fall. Websites then invent “circulating,” “locked,” “burned,” and “market cap.” Market cap uses a price. This academy will not give you a price target or a cap to worship.

For Crystal Stones, treat supply numbers you meet as **claims to verify on the contract**, not as proof of minerals. Minerals do not live in totalSupply.

TABLE
Number | Honest reading | Misreading that hurts
decimals | Display shift | “More decimals means more value”
totalSupply | Units the program currently says exist | “This is guaranteed backing”
balanceOf | Your row in this contract | “This is every chain’s USDT added up”
allowance | How much a spender may still take | “I closed the website so it is zero”
ENDTABLE

## Allowances are the quiet permission

**Allowance** is a remaining quota. After approve(router, 1000), the router may transferFrom up to 1000 units (in raw terms). If you later spend 200 yourself with transfer, the allowance is not always reduced. Designs differ. Some spenders pull max. Some approvals are the famous 2^256-1 **unlimited** number.

Revoking means sending a new approve to 0 for that spender, which is itself a transaction that costs gas. Module 6 starts with unlimited approvals because this is how adults lose tokens without losing a seed.

**Worked scenario.** Ada wants to pay a shop 15 USDT BEP-20.

1. She checks decimals on the USDT contract so 15 means 15.
2. She prefers transfer to the shop’s EOA, not approve, because the shop does not need to pull.
3. If the shop’s site demands approve, she sets 15, not unlimited.
4. After payment she reads allowance(Ada, shop). If it is not 0, she may approve 0.
5. She still pays academy tuition through academy checkout, not by approving the Crystal Stones contract.

DIAGRAM
THREE INTEGERS (stacked)

  display USDT 15.00
           ^
           | decimals = 6  (example)
           |
  storage integer 15000000   <-- balanceOf
  -------------------------------
  totalSupply integer (huge)
  -------------------------------
  allowance[Ada][Router] = 2^256-1  <-- unlimited permission
      even if Ada's balance is 15
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why “I have 0 balance so they cannot take it” fails

If you later receive tokens again, an old unlimited allowance can still be used. The permission is on the spender + owner pair, not on a particular deposit. This surprises people who thought a drained wallet was finished with a site.

## Why this lesson sits in Intermediate, not only Safety

The Basic safety course taught “do not share the seed.” This lesson is the next door: you can keep the seed in a steel box and still sign a debit order. Unlimited approval is not a hack of cryptography. It is you authorising a program, once, in a way that lasts.

People feel ashamed after a drain and then hand the rest to a recovery agent. That second loss is optional. Revoke what you can. Move remaining funds to a fresh EOA you control. Do not share the old seed or the new one. This academy will not play recovery-agent.

NOTE
Academy rule: treat unlimited approve as a standing debit order. You would not give a new shop an open debit on your bank without a reason. Do not give one to a contract you met today. Tiny amounts. Named spender. Named chain.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now read the three integers without treating the wallet as a priest. Next: USDT versus Crystal Stones versus ETH, as a comparison table you should be able to teach.

## Say this out loud

- Decimals shift a display point. The chain stores integers.
- totalSupply is the program’s count, not a mineral certificate.
- Allowance is remaining permission, and it can outlive a balance of zero.
- Unlimited approval is a standing debit order.
- Paying a shop with transfer is often simpler than approve plus pull.

Next: USDT vs Crystal Stones vs ETH — three objects Intermediate must never mash.

lessons.title: USDT vs Crystal Stones vs ETH
lessons.content:
# USDT vs Crystal Stones vs ETH

Three objects. Three jobs. One academy that will not tell you to buy any of them. If you can teach this comparison to a shopkeeper, Module 4 is working.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to place each object on the right computer, name how it moves, and name how this course is paid.

## ETH is fuel and native value on Ethereum

**ETH** is the native coin of Ethereum mainnet (chain ID 1). It pays gas there. It can be sent without a token program. It is not BNB. It is not a BEP-20. It is not Crystal Stones.

Holding ETH does not pay a BSC invoice. Holding ETH does not verify a BEP-20 contract. Holding ETH is not a requirement to study this course.

## USDT is a token family, not a unique atom

**USDT** is a **stablecoin** brand: a token designed to track the US dollar. Designed is not guaranteed. This academy will not lecture you into believing any issuer is perfect. It will say: many invoices, including **this Intermediate checkout**, ask for USDT on a named chain.

On BSC, USDT is BEP-20. On Ethereum, USDT is ERC-20. Same ticker. Different contracts. Paying $10 for this course means **USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**. If you send USDT ERC-20 on Ethereum to a BEP-20 invoice, you have not paid.

## Crystal Stones is a specific BEP-20

**Crystal Stones** is a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain. The published contract to **verify only** is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. It is not a payment address. It is not ETH. It is not USDT. It is not how you pay $10.

The project’s RWA story is their claim to verify. This classroom does not convert that claim into a vault receipt. This classroom will not tell you to buy.

TABLE
Question | ETH | USDT (as used here) | Crystal Stones
Kind | Native coin | Token (ERC-20 or BEP-20 depending on chain) | BEP-20 token
Home computer | Ethereum mainnet | Many chains — you must name one | BSC (chain 56)
Pays gas on BSC? | No | No | No
Pays this course? | No | Yes, $10 BEP-20 through academy checkout | No
Identity | Protocol ETH | A contract you must verify per chain | 0xe252… on BscScan, verify only
This academy says buy? | No | No (payment tool, not a pitch) | No
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student is offered three WhatsApp “payment addresses.”

1. Address A is an Ethereum EOA asking for ETH. Wrong object, wrong chain for this course.
2. Address B is the Crystal Stones contract. Verify-only. Not cashier.
3. Address C is a the checkout processor flow asking for USDT BEP-20. This matches the course card.
4. She checks she has BNB for gas to send that USDT.
5. She ignores a discount for paying in CS token. There is no official CS-token checkout.

DIAGRAM
THREE OBJECTS, THREE BOXES

+------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+
| ETH              |   | USDT             |   | Crystal Stones   |
| native, chain 1  |   | token, name chain|   | BEP-20, chain 56 |
| fuel on Ethereum |   | $10 Intermediate |   | verify 0xe252... |
| not BSC gas      |   | through academy checkout  |   | never cashier    |
+------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+

Do not draw arrows between boxes and call it "crypto."
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why mash-ups happen

Tickers are short. People are tired. Wallet lists are one column. Scammers rely on mash-ups: “send ETH-USDT-CS to this 0x, same thing.” It is not the same thing. Basic taught asset + network + address. Intermediate adds kind: native versus token, plus verify versus pay.

## A fourth object people sneak in: the exchange IOU

If USDT “sits on Binance” — Binance as an example of a centralised exchange — you do not hold a BEP-20 row until you withdraw to an EOA on a named chain. The IOU can be labelled USDT and still not be the contract you verified. Withdrawal is the moment kind, chain, and address become chain-real.

Do not pay Intermediate from an IOU you have not withdrawn unless the checkout processor explicitly supports that custodial flow. Do not withdraw Crystal Stones token to “convert” into tuition. Do not withdraw ETH on chain 1 to match a BSC invoice.

NOTE
Academy rule: when a token appears in this course, the next sentence is not a buy order. USDT is mentioned because invoices use it. Crystal Stones is mentioned because this academy exists around that project and must tell you how to verify it without worshipping it. ETH is mentioned because Ethereum’s computer runs on it.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The comparison is now teachable. Next: how to verify a token contract without worshipping a ticker — the practical method you will reuse on every fake.

## Say this out loud

- ETH is native on Ethereum. It is not BSC gas and not this course’s price.
- USDT is a token that must be named by chain; Intermediate wants BEP-20 through academy checkout.
- Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 to verify at 0xe252…, never a payment address.
- This academy will not tell you to buy any of the three.
- Ticker mash-ups are how $10 and $10,000 both vanish.

Next: verifying a token contract without worshipping a ticker.

lessons.title: How to verify a token contract without worshipping a ticker
lessons.content:
# How to verify a token contract without worshipping a ticker

A ticker is a nickname. Nicknames collide on purpose. Verification is a boring sequence you can do while someone is hurrying you. Hurry is part of the attack.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to run a six-step check and walk away without feeling rude.

## The six steps

1. **Name the chain.** Ethereum mainnet or BSC or something else. Write the chain ID: 1 or 56.
2. **Get the contract from more than the hurrying person.** Project site you typed, explorer search you already bookmarked, a previous lesson’s published string. For Crystal Stones: `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BSC.
3. **Paste the full address into the matching explorer.** Not a Google ad. Not a shortened link.
4. **Confirm species.** Contract tab. Token tracker. Creation tx. If it is an EOA, it is not a token contract.
5. **Confirm the interface.** Read name, symbol, decimals, totalSupply. They can still be fakes. They must at least exist if someone called it ERC-20 / BEP-20.
6. **Confirm the job.** Are you verifying, sending, or paying tuition? Tuition is the checkout processor USDT BEP-20. Verifying Crystal Stones is not paying. Sending to a person uses their EOA, not the token contract.

If any step is blocked — “no time,” “secret contract,” “use this lookalike explorer” — you stop.

## Two-source rule for Crystal Stones

For this academy’s token, one source is the published string in the lessons: `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. The second source is BscScan you typed. If a third source — a flyer, a WhatsApp status, a “listing announcement” — disagrees by one character, the third source is discarded. You do not average them. You do not send a test to both. This academy will not tell you to buy even when both honest sources match.

The RWA story, if it appears on the site, is still a claim. Matching a contract does not match a vault.

## Contract creation as a sanity check

Open the creation transaction. Note the deployer. Note the date. A token that claims to be “the original USDT” but was created last Tuesday on BSC is not the USDT a shop meant. A Crystal Stones copy created after you already saved 0xe252… is a copy. Age is not holiness. Age plus address match is a useful filter against overnight clones.

TABLE
Shortcut you will be offered | What it skips | What you do instead
“Search the ticker on BscScan” | Collision | Paste the full contract
“It’s the first MetaMask result” | Hostile token lists | Contract from a typed source
“QR from the group admin” | Species and chain | Explorer tabs
“Verified tick means official” | Audit, identity, job | Verified is compiler match only
“Pay CS to the contract to join” | Job | the checkout processor USDT BEP-20
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper is sent a Crystal Stones logo and a slightly wrong address.

1. He types BscScan himself.
2. He pastes the academy’s published verify string and the stranger’s string side by side.
3. One character differs. He does not send “a test of 1 token to see.”
4. He does not message the admin’s “support” number from the same chat.
5. He tells the group the check, without a speech about prices.

DIAGRAM
VERIFY PATH (side doors marked closed)

Typed chain ID --> typed explorer URL --> full 0x paste
        |                                      |
        v                                      v
  species + token tracker              name/symbol as labels only
        |
        v
  job: verify / pay person / pay tuition
        |
        +--> tuition: the checkout processor USDT BEP-20
        +--> verify CS: 0xe252... only
        +--> pay person: their EOA on that chain

Closed doors: ticker search, QR from hurry, lookalike explorer
ENDDIAGRAM

## What verification is not

It is not a blessing. It is not an audit. It is not proof of minerals. It is not a listing date. It is not a reason to increase size. It is matching the object on the book to the object you were told.

You still need BNB or ETH to move anything. You still need the right species. You still do not share a seed with anyone who offers to “verify for you.”

NOTE
Academy rule: verification is something you do with your own fingers on a bookmarked explorer. Anyone who needs your seed, your screen, or a prepayment to “help you verify” is not verifying. They are collecting.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 4 taught tokens as lists with a copied menu. You can now refuse ticker worship. Module 5 is the plumbing of every call: gas units, wei and gwei, ABI menus, read versus write, events as receipts.

## Say this out loud

- Tickers collide. Contracts plus chain IDs identify.
- Six steps: chain, independent 0x, explorer, species, interface, job.
- Crystal Stones verifies at 0xe252… on BscScan, never as a cashier.
- A lookalike address is a no, including for “tiny tests.”
- Hurry is a technique. Boredom is a defence.

modules.title: Gas, ABI, explorers
modules.description: Gas meters computation. wei and gwei are denominations of ETH; failed transactions still bill work. ABI is the function menu. Read does not change state; Write does. Events and logs are the public receipts of what the program claims happened.

lessons.title: Gas is fuel for computation
lessons.content:
# Gas is fuel for computation

**Gas** is the unit the EVM uses to count work. It is not naira. It is not USDT. It is a meter. You pay for the meter reading in the native coin of the computer you are using.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to split gas (the meter) from gas price (what you pay per tick) from fee (the product), and you should know why a heavy contract call costs more than a simple send.

## Three numbers, not one

A transaction quotes:

- **Gas limit** — the maximum ticks you authorise. If the call needs more, it runs out and reverts. If it needs less, unused limit is not billed the same way as used gas.
- **Gas used** — how many ticks actually happened.
- **Gas price / fee parameters** — how much native coin you pay per tick. On modern Ethereum this is a base fee plus a tip. On BSC you will still meet a gas-price picture. You do not need to become a fee-market scholar. You need: **fee ≈ gas used × price per gas, paid in ETH or BNB.**

A simple native send uses a small, known amount of gas. A contract call uses more because bytecode runs, storage may be written, other contracts may be called. That is the stack picture from Module 1 earning its keep.

TABLE
Number | What it is | What a wallet might label it
Gas limit | Cap on work | “Max fee” confusion starts here
Gas used | Work that happened | Hidden until you open the explorer
Price per gas | Native coin per tick | Gwei on Ethereum; a small BNB number on BSC
Fee | used × price | “Network fee”
Token amount | Unrelated object | Sometimes shown next to fee as if they were the same currency
ENDTABLE

## Why the network charges

If computation were free, anyone could ask every node to run infinite loops. Gas makes spam expensive and prices scarce block space. That is not a morality play. It is load control.

Cheap gas on BSC is why practice is realistic for this academy. Cheap gas is also why junk contracts thrive. Ethereum’s dearer gas does not sanctify a contract. It only changes the cost of being wrong.

**Worked scenario.** A student compares two buttons in a wallet app (an example of a wallet app, not an endorsement).

1. Button A: send BNB to an auntie. Estimated fee is small.
2. Button B: “approve and swap.” Estimated fee is larger.
3. She names why: Button B is bytecode, storage, maybe two hops.
4. She checks she has the native coin, not only the token she wants to move.
5. She does not pay a “fast lane” in Crystal Stones token to a chat address.

DIAGRAM
FEE AS A PRODUCT (not a flowchart)

  gas used (ticks of EVM work)
           x
  price per tick (native coin)
           =
  fee taken from the signing EOA

Simple send:  small used
Token transfer: more used (storage writes)
Swap:         more used (several writes + hops)
Infinite loop attempt: hits limit, reverts, still bills used work
ENDDIAGRAM

## Estimation is not a quote from a priest

Wallets estimate gas by simulating the call. Simulation can be wrong if the state changes between estimate and inclusion, or if the ABI is wrong, or if the site is lying about the contract. If the estimate is huge compared with a simple send, you are looking at a heavy program or a hostile one. If the estimate is zero, the wallet may think it is a Read, or it may be broken. Either way, you pause.

You can also set a limit too low and get “out of gas.” That fail still costs. Raising the limit a little on a known simple transfer is ordinary. Raising it into the sky on a mystery Write is paying for a longer hanging.

## Gas does not go to the shop

The fee is for the network’s writers and the protocol rules, not a tip in the token you are sending. Paying a shop 20 USDT and paying the network a little BNB are two payments that happen in one transaction. The shop does not receive the BNB gas. The network does not receive the USDT.

the checkout processor checkout for this course still needs BNB in your EOA to move the $10 USDT BEP-20. That BNB is not extra tuition. It is fuel. Do not send extra USDT “for gas” to a helper.

NOTE
Academy rule: if a stranger asks you to pay gas to a separate address before a transaction, that is a fake fee. Real gas is deducted inside the transaction from the signing EOA. Separate “gas invoices” are a Basic-level scam that still works on Intermediate students who are in a hurry.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Gas is now a meter you can talk about without saying “the network fee is magic.” Next: wei, gwei, and why a failed tx still costs — denominations and the revert bill.

## Say this out loud

- Gas is a work meter. Native coin pays the bill.
- Fee is roughly gas used times price per gas.
- Contract calls cost more than simple sends because more work happens.
- The shop receives the token; the network receives the fuel.
- Fake separate gas addresses are theft.

Next: wei, gwei, and why a “failed” transaction still costs.

lessons.title: wei, gwei, and why a "failed" tx still costs
lessons.content:
# wei, gwei, and why a "failed" tx still costs

ETH is too coarse for fees, so the chain counts in tiny fractions. **wei** is the smallest unit of ETH. **gwei** is a billion wei, the unit gas prices are often quoted in. On BSC you will meet tiny fractions of BNB instead. The moral is the same.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read a fee without panicking at a 21,000 gas number, and you should explain a failed-but-paid transaction to a shopkeeper.

## Denominations, without a maths class

1 ETH = 10^18 wei. 1 gwei = 10^9 wei. So 1 ETH = 1,000,000,000 gwei. Wallets hide this. Explorers sometimes show gas price in gwei and value in ETH. Mixing the columns is how people think they spent 21,000 ETH.

They did not. They used 21,000 **gas units** at, say, 1 gwei each, which is a small ETH fee. Gas units are ticks. Gwei is a price unit. ETH is the coin. Three columns.

BNB on BSC has its own tiny fractions (often shown as a decimal BNB fee). You do not need a new religion. You need to look at the **Fee** field on the explorer, in the native coin, after the transaction lands.

TABLE
Column | Example | Not to be confused with
Gas used | 21,000 or 85,000 | ETH amount
Gas price | 1 gwei (Ethereum example) | Token decimals
Fee | 0.000021 ETH (illustrative arithmetic, not a quote) | USDT paid to a shop
Value | 0.05 ETH sent to a person | The fee
Status | Fail | “Free”
ENDTABLE

Those fee numbers are **illustrative**, not a live oracle. This academy will not quote a price target or a “current gwei you must use.”

## Fail still included the transaction

For a transaction to show on the explorer with a hash, a block producer included it. Inclusion is work. The EVM ran until revert or until it finished. **Status: Fail** means the notebook changes from the call were undone. It does not mean the row is absent. It does not mean gas is zero.

Common fail reasons Intermediate learners actually hit:

- gas limit too low for the call
- slippage on a swap
- insufficient token row (not insufficient gas — different error)
- paused token
- wrong ABI / wrong function
- a require() in the shop contract that rejected the invoice

**Worked scenario.** Ada tries to pay 10 USDT BEP-20, the tx fails, a “support agent” appears in chat.

1. She opens BscScan, pastes the hash, sees Fail, a BNB fee, unchanged USDT row.
2. The agent says “send the leftover BNB plus your seed to unlock the refund.”
3. She names the facts: leftover BNB is still hers in her EOA; the USDT did not leave; nobody needs a seed.
4. She does not send Crystal Stones “to clear the fail.”
5. She retries later with a correct gas limit, or she uses a simple transfer instead of a hostile shop contract.

DIAGRAM
FAILED TX (before / after)

BEFORE                         AFTER FAIL
Ada BNB  0.040                 Ada BNB  0.039  (fee gone)
Ada USDT 10.00                 Ada USDT 10.00  (notebook restored)
nonce 11                       nonce 12        (tx counted)
Shop USDT 2.00                 Shop USDT 2.00

Status on explorer: Fail
Hash exists. Shop is not paid. Agent is not needed.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Out of gas is a species of fail

If the limit is too small, the call hits the wall. State reverts. Gas used can equal the limit. Wallets then say “out of gas.” Raising the limit is sometimes correct. Raising it into the sky on a hostile contract just lets the hostile contract do more work on your bill. Tiny amounts. Known contracts.

## Replacement and stuck pending

If gas price was too low, a transaction can sit **pending**. Some wallets let you speed up by sending a new transaction with the same nonce and a higher fee. That is a replacement, not a second payment of the token. If you panic and send again with a new nonce, you may pay twice when both land.

Do not accept a chat agent’s offer to “unstick” a pending tx in exchange for leftover BNB. You already have the nonce. You already have the wallet’s speed-up. This academy will not ask to remote-control that screen.

NOTE
Academy rule: a failed hash is a receipt of an attempt, not a debt to a stranger. Academy staff will not DM you because a tx failed. the checkout processor will not ask for a seed. Crystal Stones’ verify address will not “unlock” a fail.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now read denominations and failed statuses without handing the wheel to a thief. Next: ABI as the menu of functions — how wallets encode the knock on the contract’s door.

## Say this out loud

- wei and gwei are ETH fractions; gas units are work ticks; do not mix columns.
- On BSC, read the BNB fee field rather than inventing gwei folklore.
- Fail means notebook restored, meter still billed, nonce still moved.
- A support agent who needs leftover funds or a seed is a thief.
- Illustrative arithmetic is not a live gas oracle.

Next: ABI is the menu of functions — the names on the buttons, and how they can lie.

lessons.title: ABI is the menu of functions
lessons.content:
# ABI is the menu of functions

If bytecode is the kitchen, the **ABI** is the printed menu. Wallets use it to turn “transfer 10 USDT to Shop” into calldata bytes. Explorers use it to show Read and Write tabs. You already met the word in Module 3. This lesson is the working habit.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say where a healthy ABI comes from, how a pasted ABI can be hostile, and what a function selector is in beginner language.

## How a button becomes bytes

You tap Transfer. The wallet looks up the ABI line transfer(address,uint256). It encodes the shop’s address and the raw integer amount. It prefixes a **function selector** — the first four bytes of a hash of that line — so the contract knows which function you meant. That blob is **calldata**. The EVM runs bytecode, which checks the selector and proceeds.

If the ABI line is wrong, the selector is wrong, or the types are wrong, you may call a different function, or fail, or pass arguments that mean something else. Decimals mistakes live here too: 10.00 display versus 10 raw.

TABLE
ABI source | Trust level | Use
Derived from verified source on the real explorer | Best common case | Read/Write tabs, wallet auto-decode
Official library in a serious wallet for a known token | Usually fine for that token | Daily USDT send
JSON a stranger sent in chat | Hostile until proven | Do not import
ABI for a proxy without checking implementation | Incomplete | Module 6
ENDTABLE

## Pasting a hostile menu

Some “add token” or “custom contract” screens let you paste ABI. A hostile menu can label a drain function “claim refund.” You tap a kind word. Calldata selects the drain. The kitchen does what it was written to do.

Defence: prefer the explorer’s verified ABI on the address you already checked. Do not import JSON from a giveaway. Do not let a remote-control “helper” paste it for you.

**Worked scenario.** A student is asked to import an ABI to “see hidden Crystal Stones functions.”

1. She already has the verify address on BscScan.
2. If source is verified, Read/Write is already the menu.
3. Hidden functions that need a secret JSON are a red flag, not a prize.
4. She does not import. She does not pay to unlock ABI.
5. She does not send tuition to that contract. Tuition is the checkout processor.

DIAGRAM
MENU TO KITCHEN

[ ABI line: transfer(address,uint256) ]
                |
                v
[ selector (4 bytes) + encoded args ]  = calldata
                |
                v
[ bytecode kitchen ] --if match--> storage writes
                     --if not----> revert or unexpected door

A pasted ABI can print "Refund" on a drain door.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Read the names like an adult

claim, bonus, validate, sync, unlock, whitelist, migrate — these English words are not protocol words. They are labels a programmer chose. Intermediate learners look at whether the function is Write, whether it takes your tokens, whether it sets allowance, whether it is payable.

name() looking like “Tether USD” does not make the kitchen Tether. That is Module 4 again, now on the ABI tab.

## Four bytes are not a personality

The selector is short. Different function names can theoretically collide; in practice you will hit wrong-ABI more often than a hash collision. Wrong ABI is enough. If Write shows “safeTransfer” and the verified source has no such function, you are not on the menu you think.

Some wallets decode calldata back into names using a public dictionary of selectors. Dictionaries can mis-label. If the decoded name looks kind and the contract is unverified, believe the unverified part first.

Wallets also show a hex preview. If you cannot match that hex to a verified Write on the explorer for the same address, you are signing a door you have not named. That is enough reason to close the popup. Gas saved is not as valuable as the token row you would have given away.

NOTE
Academy rule: never import an ABI file from chat. Never sign a Write whose ABI you cannot see on a bookmarked explorer for that exact address. Staff will not send you a JSON menu to “complete Intermediate.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The menu is now a security object, not only a developer object. Next: Read versus Write on BscScan and Etherscan — the practical split you will use every week.

## Say this out loud

- ABI is the menu wallets encode into calldata.
- A function selector is the door code for a menu line.
- Verified explorer ABI beats a JSON from chat.
- Kind labels can sit on hostile functions.
- Crystal Stones has no hidden tuition function you must import.

Next: Read vs Write on BscScan and Etherscan.

lessons.title: Read vs write on BscScan/Etherscan
lessons.content:
# Read vs write on BscScan/Etherscan

The explorer’s Contract tab splits into **Read** and **Write** (sometimes Read as Proxy / Write as Proxy). Read asks a node to simulate a function. Write prepares a real transaction for your wallet to sign.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to use Read without connecting anything, treat Write as a live send, and know when the Proxy split matters.

## Read is a question

**Read Contract** runs view/pure style functions: balanceOf, owner, decimals, allowance. You usually do not pay gas. You do not change storage. You do not need to connect a wallet to ask many of these questions. Connecting is for the explorer’s convenience when it wants to pre-fill “your” address.

Read can still lie if you are on a fake explorer. Read can be stale by a block. Read can show the implementation’s values while you are looking at a proxy address without toggling the right tab. Even so, Read on the real BscScan or Etherscan is one of the cheapest Intermediate skills.

You can Read Crystal Stones’ published contract to confirm you are looking at a token program. That is verification. It is not a buy. It is not checkout.

## Write is a signature

**Write Contract** is a form that builds calldata and asks a wallet — Trust Wallet, MetaMask, examples only — to sign. That signature spends gas. That signature can move tokens. That signature can set allowance to a spender you did not mean if you pasted the wrong 0x in the form.

Connecting your wallet to BscScan’s Write tab is a real connection to a widely used site. Connecting it to write.bscscan.something-else is a known phishing pattern. Bookmark. Look at the URL. Prefer doing simple transfers in your wallet’s Send screen rather than the explorer Write tab until you are calm.

TABLE
Action | Tab | Gas | State change | Connect wallet?
balanceOf(Ada) | Read | No (usual) | No | No
allowance(Ada, Router) | Read | No | No | No
transfer(...) | Write | Yes | Maybe | Yes
approve(...) | Write | Yes | Maybe | Yes
owner() | Read | No | No | No
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper wants to know if a customer’s USDT row actually moved.

1. He does not open Write. He opens the transaction hash.
2. If he wants a second check, he Reads balanceOf(customer) and balanceOf(himself) on the USDT contract.
3. He does not approve the explorer. He does not approve a helper.
4. He does not Write transferFrom because a YouTube comment said that is how shops collect.
5. He settles the $10 academy question the same way: the checkout processor, not Write on Crystal Stones.

DIAGRAM
READ versus WRITE (two booths)

READ BOOTH                         WRITE BOOTH
+------------------+               +------------------+
| Ask a node       |               | Build calldata    |
| view functions   |               | Ask wallet to sign|
| no notebook edit |               | gas from EOA      |
| no seed ever     |               | can edit notebook |
+------------------+               +------------------+
URL must still be the real explorer in both booths.
Proxy toggle: Read as Proxy / Write as Proxy if the page offers it.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Proxy tabs

If the page offers **Read as Proxy**, the address you pasted is probably a thin proxy. Reading “as proxy” asks the implementation the proxy currently points at. Reading the proxy without the toggle can show almost nothing useful. Writing the proxy is how users actually interact. Module 6 explains why this is a risk, not only a UI quirk.

## Connect is not harmless chrome

When the explorer or a dApp says **Connect**, a wallet app — Trust Wallet and MetaMask are examples, not endorsements — is being asked to share an address and, later, to sign. Connect does not have to move funds. The next popup might. Use a practice EOA on a site you just met. Disconnect when the job is done. Disconnect does not revoke allowances. Revoke is a separate Write on the token.

Connecting Write on a lookalike explorer is how people sign drains while believing they are “on BscScan.” Read the domain as slowly as the amount.

NOTE
Academy rule: use Read freely on bookmarked explorers. Treat Write as a live payment. Never connect a wallet to an explorer you opened from a DM. Never paste a seed into Read, Write, or a “decoder.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a two-booth model of the Contract tab. Next: events and logs — the public receipts that make a successful call inspectable even when storage is ugly.

## Say this out loud

- Read asks; it should not spend gas or change storage.
- Write is a real transaction. URL first, then connect.
- balanceOf and allowance are Read. transfer and approve are Write.
- Proxy toggles change which kitchen you are asking.
- Crystal Stones Read is verification; Crystal Stones Write is not tuition.

Next: events and logs as the public receipt.

lessons.title: Events and logs as the public receipt
lessons.content:
# Events and logs as the public receipt

Storage is the notebook. **Logs** are the printed till receipt the program chose to emit. Wallets and explorers use those receipts to show “you sent 20 USDT” without decoding every storage slot by hand.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to find Logs on a transaction, recognise a Transfer event, and know what a receipt cannot prove.

## Events are opt-in announcements

An **event** is a structured log line bytecode can append while running. ERC-20 / BEP-20 **Transfer** is the famous one: from, to, amount. **Approval** is the other: owner, spender, amount. Indexers watch these to build the Token transfers tab.

If a hostile token moves balances in storage but does not emit Transfer, some wallets will look quiet while your row changed. If a token emits Transfer without a matching storage change, a naive indexer can be fooled for a moment. The notebook still wins. The receipt is a convenience.

## How to read a Transfer without becoming a decoder

On Logs, a decoded Transfer usually shows From, To, Amount, and the contract that emitted it. Check the contract first. Then To. Then Amount after decimals. Then Status of the parent transaction. Four fields, same as the shopkeeper check in Module 2.

A swap will emit more than one Transfer: you → pool, pool → you, maybe a fee to a third address. That is expected. A payment to a person should usually show one Transfer to their EOA (or to the invoice contract they named). Extra Transfers to an unknown 0x are a reason to pause, not a reason to invent a story.

On the explorer, open a tx, then **Logs**. You will see topics (indexed fields) and data. You do not need to parse hex for this course. You need to know the tab exists, and that a Transfer log to your EOA is the usual public receipt of a token payment.

TABLE
Receipt you might trust | What it is | What it is not
Transfer log to your EOA | Program announced a token move | Proof the token is USDT the shop meant
Success status | Call did not revert | Proof you used the right chain next time
the checkout processor invoice paid | Their system saw the USDT BEP-20 | A Crystal Stones transfer
Screenshot of a log | A picture | The book
Internal tx of BNB | Native coin hop | A token payment
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Ada is waiting for a client to pay 50 USDT BEP-20.

1. Client sends a hash.
2. Ada opens BscScan, Status Success, Logs, Transfer, destination = her EOA, contract = the USDT she verified, amount = 50 after decimals.
3. If the log’s contract is a lookalike, she has not been paid in the USDT she prices goods in.
4. If there is no Transfer log and her balanceOf did not rise, she has not been paid.
5. She will not accept a Crystal Stones Transfer log as academy tuition.

DIAGRAM
TWO PUBLIC RECORDS

STORAGE (notebook)                 LOGS (till receipt)
Ada's USDT row: 50                 Transfer(from Client, to Ada, 50)
Shop's USDT row:  3                Approval(...) maybe none

Indexers read logs to paint wallet screens.
If logs and storage disagree, storage is the money.
If the contract is a fake, both can look "successful."
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why Intermediate needs receipts

Because shops get screenshots. Because failed txs still have hashes. Because swaps emit several Transfer logs in one tx. Because you can see an Approval log and finally understand that yesterday’s “connect” was a standing debit order.

## Approval logs are receipts of permission, not of payment

An **Approval** event says a quota was set. It does not say tokens moved. Shopkeepers who accept an Approval screenshot as payment have accepted a debit order picture. Ada can approve a router for 50 USDT and never transfer. The shop is not paid. the checkout processor is not paid. The explorer is not confused; the human is.

You also need the limit: logs are not a court. They are not an audit. They are not mineral proof. They are what the program shouted while it ran.

NOTE
Academy rule: for payments, match four fields on the real explorer — success, token contract, destination, amount. The log tab is how you see those fields for tokens. Do not take a picture of a log from a stranger as a substitute.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 5 gave you meter, denominations, menu, read/write, and receipts. Module 6 is how this design actually hurts people — approvals, fakes, verified-not-audited, proxies, and the practice rules for this paid track.

## Say this out loud

- Events are opt-in log lines; Transfer is the token receipt.
- Indexers paint wallets from logs; storage is still the money.
- A lookalike token can emit a perfect-looking Transfer.
- Match success, contract, destination, amount.
- Crystal Stones logs are not the checkout processor tuition receipts.

Next: unlimited token approval — the standing debit order that empties wallets without stealing a seed.
