lessons.title: Unlimited token approval
lessons.content:
# Unlimited token approval

You can lose tokens without losing your seed. The usual door is **approve** with a huge number. The spender then uses **transferFrom** whenever they like, until you revoke, or until the row is empty and later refilled.

By the end of this lesson you should treat unlimited approval as a standing debit order, know how to read it, and know how to set it towards zero.

## Why sites ask for max

User-experience: they do not want to prompt you every trade. Gas: one approval instead of many. Honesty: sometimes. Laziness: often. Hostility: enough that this lesson exists.

The unlimited number is often 2^256−1. Wallets may show “unlimited” or a comic-strip of nines. Either way, the allowance map in the token contract now says that spender may pull more than you will ever hold.

A later “drain” transaction is not a mystery. It is transferFrom succeeding because you already signed the debit order. The explorer will show your EOA as the token From even though a contract pulled it. That screenshot ruins people who think they were hacked in the seed-phrase sense. They were hacked in the permission sense.

TABLE
Permission style | What you signed | Typical after
Exact amount | Spender may take up to that remaining quota | Safer for a one-off shop
Unlimited | Spender may take until you revoke | Convenient; standing risk
Zero (revoke) | Spender quota set to 0 | Costs gas; worth it after a throwaway site
Permit / typed signature | A gasless-looking allowance message | Still a permission; still readable later
ENDTABLE

## How to see it and how to shrink it

Read allowance(your EOA, spender) on the token contract. Token approval checkers exist as websites; they are extra phishing surface. If you use one, type the URL, use a tiny wallet, and still confirm on BscScan or Etherscan.

To revoke, Write approve(spender, 0) on the **same token contract**, or use your wallet’s built-in revoke if it has one. That is a transaction. It costs native coin. It is not a customer-care ticket. It does not need a seed shared with a helper.

**Worked scenario.** Ada connected a swap site on BSC last month.

1. She Reads USDT allowance(Ada, that router). The number is unlimited.
2. She does not have a trade open. She approves 0, pays a little BNB.
3. She Reads again. Zero.
4. She notices a second spender she does not remember. She revokes that too.
5. She never approved Crystal Stones as a way to pay Intermediate. She uses the checkout processor when tuition is the job.

DIAGRAM
STANDING DEBIT (before / after revoke)

BEFORE                             AFTER approve(spender, 0)
USDT storage                       USDT storage
  Ada balance  80                    Ada balance  80
  allowance[Ada][Router] = max       allowance[Ada][Router] = 0

Router can transferFrom            Router call should fail
anytime Ada holds USDT             (unless she approves again)
ENDDIAGRAM

## What revoke does not fix

It does not bring back tokens already pulled. It does not find a thief. It does not replace a seed that was already stolen. It does not pay tuition. It does not make a fake token honest.

If the spender is a proxy, revoking the proxy address is the usual target. If you revoke the old implementation, you may have missed the door.

## Phishing sits on top of the same function

“Claim airdrop” sites are often approve() with a kind label. The ABI says drain. The wallet may summarise “Allow access to USDT.” That English is already too soft. Read spender and amount. If amount is unlimited and you do not know the spender’s 0x from an independent source, you do not sign.

Permit-style signatures (gasless allowance messages) are still allowances. They can be phished too. If you did not mean to authorise a spender, do not sign a typed message you cannot read.

NOTE
Academy rule: first meeting with a contract, cap the approval at the amount of this job. Revoke when the job is over if you do not need a standing connection. Practice this on tiny amounts before you ever hold a month’s fees in a token row.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The permission door is now named. Next: fake tokens with the same name — the identity door that sits next to it.

## Say this out loud

- Unlimited approve is a standing debit order on a token row.
- Drains via transferFrom often look like you sent the tokens.
- Read allowance; write approve(spender, 0) to revoke; it costs gas.
- Revoke does not undo a completed pull.
- Do not approve Crystal Stones or a mystery spender as academy checkout.

Next: fake tokens with the same name — why the ticker is bait.

lessons.title: Fake tokens with the same name
lessons.content:
# Fake tokens with the same name

If name() is free to copy, it will be copied. USDT, ETH, Crystal Stones, the checkout processor, Binance — the nicknames are public. The contracts are not interchangeable.

By the end of this lesson you should refuse ticker search as identity, and you should know the usual delivery tricks: airdrops, lookalike addresses, and “support” tokens sitting in the wallet.

## How the fake arrives

**Airdrop.** A contract credits your address without asking. Your wallet shows a new row with a familiar logo. Tapping it opens a site. The site asks for approve or a seed. The airdropped units were bait, not a gift.

**Lookalike address.** One character off Crystal Stones’ `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. Hurry does the rest.

**Wrong chain, right ticker.** USDT ERC-20 offered when the invoice was BEP-20. The send can succeed on the wrong book.

**Wallet token lists.** Some lists are crowdsourced. First result is not a notary. Adding by contract is slower and safer.

## The one-character address

Humans are bad at hex. Scammers generate addresses that share the first six and last four characters of a famous contract. Wallet UIs often truncate the middle. Always expand. Always compare the middle. Crystal Stones is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` — the whole string, on BSC, verify only.

If a QR code is offered, decode it to text and compare. QR is not a cryptographic proof of identity. It is a drawing of a string.

TABLE
Bait | What you see | What you do
Airdrop named USDT | Extra row, maybe a “claim” button | Ignore; do not approve; do not visit the linked site
CS copycat | Same logo, different 0x | Compare every character to the published verify string
Invoice on Ethereum | USDT ticker | Ask chain ID; Intermediate checkout is BEP-20
“Official pool” QR | A contract | Species check; job check; tiny test to a known EOA only if paying a person
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** An auntie’s wallet shows 40,000 “Crystal Stones.”

1. She does not celebrate. She does not sell. This academy will not tell her to buy or sell.
2. She opens BscScan, token tracker for that row’s contract.
3. It is not 0xe252…. She leaves the row alone. Hiding a token in the wallet is cosmetic, not required.
4. She does not click Claim. She does not DM the number in the airdrop memo.
5. She still pays tuition, if she owes it, through academy checkout USDT BEP-20.

DIAGRAM
SAME NAME, DIFFERENT NOTEBOOKS

Wallet list (one column of tickers)
  USDT
  USDT     <-- copycat
  Crystal Stones
  Crystal Stones  <-- airdrop bait
  ETH      <-- a token named ETH on BSC, not native ETH

Explorer identity (what actually matters)
  chain 56 + 0x...USDT-real
  chain 56 + 0xe252...  (CS verify only)
  chain 1  + native ETH
ENDDIAGRAM

## Do not “test send” to a copycat to see

A test send to a thief still arrives. A test send to a copycat contract may stick. Tests are for destinations you already independently identified, in tiny size. They are not for curiosity about malware.

Binance, as an example of a centralised exchange, will not airdrop you a random CS token and then ask you to “validate” it. Wallet apps will not. This academy will not.

## Hide versus send versus approve

Hiding a junk token in a wallet is cosmetic. Sending it “back” can approve a drain site. Selling it on a random pool can interact with a hostile pair. The least dramatic action is no action. You do not have to clean the screen. You do have to avoid the buttons that say Claim, Validate, or Convert.

If you accidentally approved the bait token’s spender on your USDT, that is a USDT problem. Revoke the USDT allowance. The bait row can stay.

Copycats of Crystal Stones will reuse the logo, the RWA paragraph, and sometimes a screenshot of BscScan with the real 0xe252… in the image and a different 0x in the pay button. Read the button. Do not read the JPEG. This academy will not tell you to buy the real one either; verification is not a shopping list.

NOTE
Academy rule: a surprise token is not a paycheck. It is either dust, a mistake, or bait. You do not owe it a click. You do not owe it an approval. You do not owe it a conversation.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Ticker bait is now boring, which is the goal. Next: verified source is not an audit — the trust badge that is only a compiler match.

## Say this out loud

- name() and logos copy. Contracts plus chain IDs identify.
- Airdrops are often bait for approve or phishing sites.
- Compare Crystal Stones to 0xe252… on BscScan, every character.
- Do not test-send to an unidentified 0x.
- Surprise tokens are not tuition and not a buy signal.

Next: verified source is not an audit.

lessons.title: Verified source is not an audit
lessons.content:
# Verified source is not an audit

BscScan and Etherscan can print a green **Verified** badge. That badge means a compiler match. Adults still point at it as if a firm of auditors slept at the contract. They did not.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what verification is, what an audit is, and what neither of them is.

## Verification, again, as a small object

Someone uploaded source. The explorer compiled it with a stated compiler version and settings. The bytecode matched what is on chain (or matched a flattened/creation result under their rules). You can now read Solidity instead of hex. That is the whole gift.

Verification does not test whether transfer taxes users. It does not test whether owner can mint. It does not test whether a proxy can swap kitchens. It does not test whether the team’s mineral vault exists. It does not insure you.

## Audit is a human review, and still limited

An **audit** is a report by people who read the source (sometimes) and look for bugs. Good audits are useful. They have dates. They have scope (“we looked at these files”). They miss things. They go stale when the program is upgraded. They can be forged as PDFs. They can be bought as logos.

If a project waves an audit, you still ask: which address, which chain, which date, which files, and did the code change after. You do not take a Telegram screenshot of a badge. This academy is not your auditor. This academy will not “confirm” Crystal Stones as audited because a file was pretty.

## Who paid for the PDF

Audits are paid work. That does not make every auditor a liar. It does mean the customer chose the firm, the scope, and whether to publish the ugly bits. A two-page “certificate” with no findings and no file list is marketing. A long report that says “owner can mint” and a website that hides that sentence are a mismatch. Believe the report’s findings over the banner.

Verification and audit can both be absent on a useful program. Absence is fog. Fog is a reason to keep size tiny or to walk away, not a reason to trust a Telegram admin who “knows the devs.” The EVM will run unverified bytecode as calmly as verified bytecode. The badge is for you, not for the processor.

If Crystal Stones is verified on BscScan when you look, that helps you read functions. It does not pay tuition. It does not prove minerals. It does not make a copycat with a green tick on a fake explorer into the same object.

TABLE
Badge | Precise meaning | Not the meaning
Verified on explorer | Source compiled to bytecode | Safe, official, insured
Audit PDF | Humans reviewed a scope at a date | Forever-safe, covers upgrades
KYC badge on a random site | Someone checked an identity somewhere | Honest token
Listed on an exchange | An example CEX or DEX offered a pair | Quality
Academy mention | Education, verify-only contract | Buy order, audit, vault proof
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student is told “it is verified, send freely.”

1. She accepts verification as readability.
2. She still Reads owner, mint, pause, tax if those functions exist.
3. She still caps approvals.
4. She still does not send rent.
5. She still will not pay Intermediate in CS token because a badge was green.

DIAGRAM
BADGE STACK (bottom is weaker than people think)

Layer 5  "Therefore buy"          <-- academy never says this
Layer 4  Audit of today's proxy   <-- maybe, check date + address
Layer 3  Audit of last year's code
Layer 2  Verified source (compiler match)
Layer 1  Bytecode exists on a public chain

You can stand on layer 2 and still fall through layer 4.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this academy will verify, and stop

We will repeat Crystal Stones’ published BEP-20 address so you can match it. We will repeat that Intermediate is $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout. We will repeat that staff never need a seed. We will not convert those sentences into an audit of the token, the team, or the RWA claim.

NOTE
Academy rule: green ticks are not parents. If a lesson ever sounded like “verified therefore deposit,” the lesson failed. Read the functions. Size the risk at amounts you can lose. Walk away often.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The badge hierarchy is now explicit. Next: proxies and upgradeable contracts — how the kitchen can move after you read it.

## Say this out loud

- Verified means compiler match, not audit.
- Audits have scope and dates and can go stale after upgrades.
- Badges can be copied in PDFs and group chats.
- Crystal Stones mention here is verify-only education, not an audit stamp.
- Green is not a buy, not tuition, not a vault receipt.

Next: proxies and upgradeable contracts — the moving kitchen.

lessons.title: Proxies and upgradeable contracts
lessons.content:
# Proxies and upgradeable contracts

You can read last month’s source and still be calling this month’s kitchen. That is the **proxy** pattern: a stable address that delegates to an **implementation** contract the admin can change.

By the end of this lesson you should recognise proxy tabs on an explorer, know why projects use them, and know the extra question: **who can point this address at new bytecode?**

## Two contracts, one public door

Users send calls to the **proxy** address. The proxy stores the notebook (usually) and forwards the call to the implementation using a special EVM mechanism (delegatecall, in the common pattern). **Delegatecall** means: run that other contract’s code against *this* storage. The user keeps talking to one 0x. The team can later set a new implementation.

That is convenient for fixing bugs. It is also how an “audited” door becomes a new program. If the admin key is compromised, the new program can be a drain. If the admin is the attacker, verification of the old source is theatre.

Explorers try to help: “Proxy,” “Read as Proxy,” implementation address, admin address. Use those tabs. If a site gives you a token address and the explorer says proxy, you are not done.

TABLE
Object | Job | Failure if ignored
Proxy address | The door users call; often holds storage | You verified a different 0x
Implementation | The current kitchen code | You read yesterday’s kitchen
Proxy admin | Who may switch kitchens | “Immutable” was a slogan
User-facing token tracker | Convenience | Tracker may lag an upgrade
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A shopkeeper is invited to “deposit into the upgraded vault, same address as last year.”

1. He opens the address on the matching explorer.
2. He sees Proxy. He notes implementation and admin.
3. He checks whether admin is a multisig or a single EOA. A single EOA is a single point of betrayal or theft.
4. He does not deposit school fees. He does not trust “same address” as “same rules.”
5. He does not pay academy tuition through that vault. Tuition is the checkout processor.

DIAGRAM
PROXY CUTAWAY (side by side)

DOOR (proxy 0xDoor)              KITCHEN (implementation 0xImpl)
+----------------------+         +----------------------+
| storage notebook     |  <----- | bytecode (logic)     |
| balances, owner      |  run    | can be replaced      |
| implementation slot  |  here   | users rarely call it |
| admin slot           |         |                      |
+----------------------+         +----------------------+
        ^
        |
   users keep calling 0xDoor
   admin can point implementation slot at 0xImpl-NEW
ENDDIAGRAM

## Not all upgrades are crimes

Software has bugs. Honest teams want a patch path. Intermediate is not a purity contest. It is a labelling contest. Call it an upgradeable product. Do not call it unstoppable code. Size deposits as if a company could change the rules — because, at the admin layer, it can.

Some proxies are **immutable** in practice if admin was burned. “Burned” is a claim you verify by reading the admin slot, not by reading a tweet. Even then, related contracts (bridges, routers) may still be upgradeable.

## Implementation addresses can be unverified

A verified proxy can point at unverified bytecode. The door looks readable. The kitchen is fog. Intermediate habit: open the implementation address too. If that page has no source, you have not read the rules. Do not deposit because the proxy’s ABI looks friendly.

A new implementation can also be verified and still hostile. Verification is readability. Admin is power. Both can be true on a public chain.

## initializer instead of constructor

Upgradeable kitchens often cannot use a normal constructor the way a simple contract does, because the proxy’s storage is the notebook. They use an **initializer** function that should run once. If it can run twice, an attacker may seize owner. You will not audit that in this course. You will notice “initialize” on Write and treat a second call as a danger sign, not as a setup wizard you must complete.

NOTE
Academy rule: if the explorer says Proxy, add one question to your checklist — who can change the implementation, and how fast. If you cannot answer, you are using a product with a hidden patch panel. Tiny amounts until you can answer.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The moving kitchen is now visible. Last lesson: practice rules for Intermediate — testnet, tiny amounts, and never CS token as checkout.

## Say this out loud

- A proxy is a stable door that can point at a new kitchen.
- Delegatecall runs other code against this storage.
- Admin keys make “I read the source” time-stamped, not eternal.
- Same address after an upgrade is not the same program.
- Do not deposit rent in an upgradeable vault you cannot explain.

Next: practice rules for Intermediate — how to use this $10 course without becoming the failure case.

lessons.title: Practice rules for Intermediate (testnet, tiny amounts, never CS token as checkout)
lessons.content:
# Practice rules for Intermediate (testnet, tiny amounts, never CS token as checkout)

A $10 course is still a course. It is not a dare to empty a salary into a proxy. This last lesson writes the rules of motion for everything you just learned.

By the end you should be able to quote how you will practice, how you will pay, and what staff will never ask.

## Testnet is a practice computer

A **testnet** is a public network that copies the shape of a main computer and uses worthless play coins. Ethereum has testnets. BSC has testnets. Explorers exist for them. Faucets give play native coin. Contracts you deploy there do not make you a protocol engineer. They let you see Fail, gas, ABI, and logs without bleeding.

Mainnet is chain ID 1 (Ethereum) or 56 (BSC). Do not mix a testnet USDT with a mainnet academy checkout invoice. Play coins do not pay $10 tuition. They also do not turn into Crystal Stones.

If a faucet asks for a seed, it is not a faucet. If a “testnet helper” wants remote control, they are not a helper.

## Tiny amounts on mainnet

When you must use mainnet — a real USDT invoice, a real shop, this course — size the first send at an amount that would annoy you, not ruin you. Wait for the explorer. Then send the rest. This is the same rule as Basic, now applied to contract calls and approvals.

Keep a separate practice EOA if you can manage the extra seed **offline**. Do not practice drains on the account that holds rent. Do not import that practice seed into random apps.

## One job per session

When you sit down to practice, name the job in a sentence: “I will Read balanceOf on BscScan,” or “I will send 1 USDT test to the shopkeeper,” or “I will pay $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.” Mixing jobs is how people approve a swap while meaning to pay tuition. Close extra dApp tabs. Disconnect when finished. Revoke if the job was a one-off pull.

If the job is verification of Crystal Stones, the session ends when the address matches. No send. No wrap. No buy. This academy will not tell you to buy.

TABLE
Move | Where | Size | Never
Learn Fail / gas / logs | Testnet | Play coins | Seed to a faucet
Learn a new shop’s USDT address | Mainnet BSC | Tiny test then the rest | Wrong chain “because 0x matches”
Pay Intermediate | Mainnet BSC | $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout | CS token, ETH, random 0x
Verify Crystal Stones | BscScan | Zero value required | Sending to 0xe252… as payment
Revoke an allowance | Mainnet | Gas only | Helper who needs remaining tokens
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student finished Module 6 and is ready to pay.

1. She confirms the course card: $10, USDT BEP-20, the checkout processor.
2. She checks BNB for gas on chain 56 in her EOA.
3. She ignores a Discord discount: “pay 5 CS to the contract.”
4. She does not send USDT to `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`.
5. She completes the checkout processor, then uses the course. She still will not be asked for a seed to “activate.”

DIAGRAM
ALLOWED PATHS versus CLOSED PATHS

ALLOWED
  [ Testnet play tx ] --> learn Fail, logs, ABI
  [ Tiny mainnet test ] --> then rest to a known EOA
  [ $10 USDT BEP-20 ] --> the checkout processor --> Intermediate access
  [ BscScan paste 0xe252... ] --> verify only

CLOSED
  [ CS token ] --> 0xe252... "cashier"
  [ ETH on chain 1 ] --> a chat invoice for this course
  [ Seed phrase ] --> staff / faucet / explorer
  [ Unlimited approve ] --> first meeting with a site
ENDDIAGRAM

## The never list, in one place

- Never send Crystal Stones token as checkout. The contract is verify-only.
- Never treat 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 as a payment address.
- Never pay this course in ETH because “Ethereum is the real computer.”
- Never give a seed, private key, 2FA code, or remote screen to anyone, including people who name this academy.
- Never import ABI JSON from chat.
- Never skip chain ID.
- Never confuse verified with audited, or audited with “deposit your year.”

This academy will not tell you to buy ETH, BNB, USDT as an investment, or Crystal Stones. USDT appears as an invoice currency. BNB appears as BSC fuel. ETH appears as Ethereum’s native coin. Crystal Stones appears as a BEP-20 to verify.

NOTE
Academy rule: Intermediate skill is restraint plus naming. If you can name the computer, the species of account, the drawer you are filling, the menu line you are signing, and the job (practice, pay a person, pay the checkout processor, verify), you are ready to use this track. If you cannot name them, you wait. Waiting is a pass, not a fail.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

This is the operating manual. The quiz will check whether the failure cases stuck. You do not need a price. You need the reflex.

## Say this out loud

- Testnet is for learning Fail and logs with play coins, not for paying $10.
- Mainnet practice is tiny, then the rest, on a named chain.
- Intermediate checkout is $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout only.
- Crystal Stones’ contract is verify-only, never a cashier.
- Staff never ask for seed, key, 2FA, or remote control — if someone does, they are not staff.

You now have the six modules. Take the quiz. Then go back to any explorer tab that still feels like fog and read it once more, slowly.
